subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, November 8, consideration of the motion of Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the past week of this debate we have heard many opposition members rise in this house and declare that they were not at all satisfied with the 2 per cent tax with a $120 limit. I must say that when I first heard the minister announce this tax I had the same reaction. Like some other members I felt that this tax would bear more heavily on the middle income groups and favour more the upper income groups. As a result of my first reaction to the announcement I saw the minister and, with some others, I suggested that maybe a 1 per cent or a less than 1 per cent tax, without limit, would be preferable.
However, Mr. Speaker, having studied these alternatives and worked them out mathematically I have become less warm to my original proposals. I have found that if we were to raise through a percentage tax without any limit, the same amount of money as we now wish to raise, the tax would come to approximately 1.65 per cent, which is not too much different from 2 per cent. If we apply it to a married man earning $5,000 a year, with two children, we find the difference in his tax is only $8 per year. In other words, if the tax were 1.65 per cent without any limit rather than 2 per cent with a limit, the man earning
DEBATES	2635
The Budget-Mr. Allmand $5,000 per year, with two children, would pay only $8 less a year.
On the other hand, balanced against this we would have a system whereby those in the upper tax bracket would pay a greatly increased rate of tax, and this is a group already paying tax under a rapidly increasing progressive tax system. I would like to remind the house what those progressive rates of taxes are. A person who has a taxable income of $4,000 a year, that is, taxable income after exemptions and so forth, pays $610 per year plus 22 per cent on the next $2,000. A person with $8,000 taxable income per year pays at least a basic $1,570 tax plus 30 per cent on the next $2,000. If we move up to $12,000 taxable income a person pays $2,870 basic tax, plus 40 per cent on the next $3,000. Jumping up to $25,000 a year taxable income a person pays a basic $8,570 tax, plus 50 per cent on the remaining $15,000, and if we go to $60,000 a year taxable income a person pays a basic $27,000 tax, plus 60 per cent on the next $30,000. We note, Mr. Speaker, that the rates of taxation increase by a very progressive measure.
Comparing the rates of taxation in Canada for different groups with the rates of taxation in the United States the Carter commission noted that a married taxpayer in Canada making more than $10,000 per year paid higher rates of taxes than his counterpart in the United States, and a married taxpayer in Canada earning less than $10,000 per year paid a smaller rate of tax than his counterpart in the United States. It was suggested that the rates of tax in Canada for the managerial and entrepreneurial classes should not be such that they would be an additional factor in luring Canadians to other countries.
We know how easy it is for skilled Canadians, for Canadian graduates, to go to the United States. Most of them speak the same language as the people of the United States. Basically in many respects they have the same culture and it is easy for them to migrate to the United States and make a living there. It was suggested that for the managerial income groups the rates of tax in Canada should be somewhat similar to the rates of tax in the United States and that in the long run this would be in the general economic interests of Canada.
When doing research in preparation for this debate I noticed another very interesting point. In recent days when the opposition has talked about the government we have heard much about a credibility gap. I would like to
November 12, 1968

The Budget-Mr. Allmand suggest there are even greater credibility gaps with respect to the opposition parties, comparing what they say and what they in fact do.
If we look at the record of the C.C.F.-New Democratic party in Saskatchewan when it introduced a medical insurance program in the early 1960's and joined it with the hospitalization program, the New Democratic party decided that the program should be paid for by a flat rate premium which was to be the same for the lower income group, the middle income group and the upper income group. I believe that premium is now $36 per year for an individual and $72 per year for a family. If it is unfair and unjust to the middle income group to have a 2 per cent tax with a limit of $120 then I submit it is much more unfair and unjust to have a flat rate premium which is a much greater percentage of income for the lower income group than it is for the middle and upper income groups.
It so happens that the leader of the New Democratic party was the premier of Saskatchewan when that flat rate premium was introduced, and it is of note that he is at present campaigning in British Columbia to get a seat in this house. No doubt he will be attacking this 2 per cent tax and saying it is unjust and unfair. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the candidate for my party, the Liberal party, should bring to the attention of the voters in the British Columbia constituency that what he introduced as payment for a similar program in Saskatchewan was much more arduous on the lower income groups than it was on the middle and upper income groups.
The opposition parties may say that that premium did not cover and was not intended to cover the entire cost of the hospitalization and medical care program. They would be correct in saying that, but the 2 per cent tax that we are applying, with a limit of $120, is also not meant to cover the entire cost of the hospitalization program, the medical care program and the supplements provided for the post-secondary educational system. So, Mr. Speaker, I submit that there is a credibility gap so far as the opposition parties are concerned, particularly the N.D.P., in the way they attack this particular tax because they say one thing but when they are in charge of government they do another thing.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Let us look at the taxes which other countries in the world pay for similar programs. In England, under the national health service

there is a flat rate premium system. In Sweden 50 per cent of their program is paid by a flat rate premium system. Some other countries, however, have a progressive tax to pay for their hospitalization, medicare and social welfare programs. In every one I examined there is a limit. I can give examples. In West Germany there is a special tax premium ranging from 5 per cent to 10 per cent of wages per month for the health program. They have a limit on that of 660 Deutsch marks per month. In France the tax for the hospitalization and medicare program is 6 per cent of wages and they have a ceiling of 700 new francs per month. In making a study of these programs it became apparent that in every case there was either a flat rate premium program or a percentage or graduated premium program, but there was no case in which there was not a limit. In respect of Sweden I have an article entitled "Socialized Medicine In Sweden"-

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

speechtext: Yes.

speechtext: Is the hon. member suggesting that the so-called social development tax of 2 per cent is connected with a specific government program, for example, medicare?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister stated that the social development tax which was introduced was to pay for large deficits in the shared cost programs, especially post-secondary education and hospitalization and the medicare program which was to be introduced. That was my understanding of it. It is called a social development tax.
I was about to quote from an article entitled "Socialized Medicine In Sweden", to be found in the publication Current History, January, 1963, at page 336. It reads as follows:
The general health insurance costs are not fully met by public outlay, national or local. Since 1955, when the present compulsory insurance law went into effect, approximately 50 per cent of the cost has been covered by individual premium payments, 25 per cent by contributions coming from the employer and 25 per cent by the public treasury which means, obviously, by taxpayers. Referring to this distribution of costs, Karl J. Hojer, former director of Sweden's Royal Social Board, started in 1959 that by the early 1950's it had become clear "that direct taxes in Sweden had become so high, especially on upper incomes, that any attempt to apply further pressure would have dangerous effects." A situation "had been reached where a transfer by taxation
November 12, 1968	COMMONS
of money from the higher income groups to the lower income groups, in the form of social benefits for the latter, could not be pursued any further."
I know that in Sweden the rate of taxation in the higher income groups is greater than it is in Canada, but I cite that article to point out that in all the countries in western Europe that I have studied which have these programs they have seen fit to have a limit where they have a progressive rate of taxation in addition to specialized taxes. That is the main point of my referring to these articles.
I also should like to refer to some of the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). In his speech last week he made the statement that there is a great credibility gap with regard to the government and its predictions concerning the estimates and so on. I submit that there is an even greater credibility gap with regard to the opposition, especially since it has been led by the present Leader of the Opposition.
In the period of approximately one year since the Leader of the Opposition came here he has consistently criticized the government for not properly controlling costs and for not properly controlling spending programs. Yet, whenever the government has brought forward proposals to control those costs and cut down on the spending program, either the Leader of the Opposition or members of his party have risen in this house and criticized these cuts. When the minister of finance brought forward proposals last spring in respect of certain cuts in costs, immediately there were complaints from the Conservative opposition about cuts in shipbuilding subsidies, in the subsidies to the cheese industry and about the review of the Prince Edward Island causeway program which was brought up again today. This fall we have had criticism about the cut in the observatory program in British Columbia, about the winter works program and about the cut in the atomic energy program. I am not saying that these are not good programs and perhaps have merit, but I am trying to point out that there is a real inconsistency in the approach of the opposition and a real credibility gap. They cannot have it both ways.

When the public accounts committee met last year a recommendation was made which was fully supported by the Conservative members of that committee. The recommendation was with regard to second class mail. In its recommendation the committee said:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as this is the first occasion I have had to speak in this house since my election to represent the riding of Palliser, may I take this opportunity of congratulating you on your re-election as the presiding officer of the house. I should also like to congratulate your deputy, the chairman of committees, and the deputy chairman of committees on their accession to those offices and to say that they are proving to be happy choices for those positions.
The Palliser electoral district is situated in that part of the province of Alberta which lies to the west, north and east of the city of Calgary. The riding also includes a large portion of the city of Calgary and the Indian reserve of the Sarcee tribe. As a result, in the Palliser constituency can be found examples of most kinds of agricultural enterprise ranging from ranching, dairy farming and mixed farming through to some of the most productive grain farms to be found in this country. This is an area that has produced several world wheat kings in recent years.
In this my first contribution to the debates of this house I had hoped to be as helpful and
November 12, 1968	COMMONS
as uncritical as possible. I still hope I can be helpful, but I can no longer be uncritical. In the face of the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), Pollyanna would be driven into an acute state of depression and Anne of Green Gables would be moved to profanity. It is, in my view, the most negative, defeatist and depressing statement made to the Canadian people in recent times.
It is defeatist because it admits nothing can be done to correct the shameful state into which federal finances have been allowed to fall in five years of Liberal rule. It is negative because it inhibits any progressive legislation in the field of national development and effectively prevents the creation of any new national wealth or the formation of a wider and stronger tax base. It is depressing because it seeks to give the philsophy of doom and gloom the sanction of the Canadian parliament, and squeezes the tax collar tighter around the necks of the already choking taxpayer, particularly those in the lower and middle income areas. It is a sorry day when, in the midst of unparalleled affluence, our Minister of Finance can offer nothing but rising debt and taxes.
This budget clearly mirrors the blind grop-ings of a minister driven by the compulsion to find some way out of the mess and stave off bankruptcy. There is something reminiscent today of the period immediately prior to the outbreak of the French revolution. You may recall that the great banker, Jacques Necker, was called back to bring order out of the chaos of Louis XVI's financial world. He failed and the revolution followed. Necker was exiled and the king lost his head. I am not suggesting that we will shortly face a violent revolution in this country, but actions such as those of this government, as reflected in this barren budget, could bring on a revolution of a milder sort.
Aside from the bitter disappointment created by this budget, apart from the sudden death it brought to the promises and hopes of a just society, of new national goals and a new spirit of national purpose, its most unpleasant aspect is the financial bumbling and inadequacy demonstrated by the minister's explanation of its provisions.
The greatest irony is his repeated plea for cut-backs in spending, for economy at all levels and for belt tightening and austerity. It is ironic because those who cry loudest for austerity are the very ones guilty of the most extravagant spending. If only one of his

The Budget-Mr. Schumacher colleagues practised what the Minister of Finance preaches we could save a considerable bag of tax dollars. The cabinet's taste for high living is well known and has been frequently mentioned in this house already, but there are many other areas of expenditure where lack of common sense and restraint make a mockery of the minister's plea for economy and the painful provisions of this budget.
Recently the Minister of Finance sent the representatives of the provinces packing without even carfare home. He denied them any extra money to help them in the discharge of their responsibilities. He shut them out from any share in the harvest of tax dollars that this new budget is designed to scoop up. He particularly slammed the door on the provinces' sharing in the 2 per cent social development tax, although most of the measures he claimed came under social development. These had been foisted on the ill-prepared and financially strapped provinces by the federal government by what amounts to fiscal blackmail.
The Minister of Finance is Canada's most outspoken advocate of austerity, but what is happening in his own backyard? While he is in the pulpit preaching, his colleagues are robbing the poor box. There is no trouble finding funds for the pet projects of various ministers. There is lots of money to finance the B and B commission and to set up an expensive new bureaucracy under a language commissar. But scientific and research projects vital to the development of the nation are ruthlessly lopped off. Last year HARP, the high altitude research project, was killed, and this year the Queen Elizabeth telescope and ING, the intense neutron generator project, were scrapped in the name of economy in government spending.

But there has been no change in the blank cheque policy of financing the National Arts Centre, which has been characterized by one of the members of the treasury benches as a "$47 million dance hall". There are ample funds for the lavish redecoration of ministerial offices. There is plenty of cash to build up the personal staff of cabinet members, including the largest prime ministerial staff in history. What happened to the freeze on the civil service? Is this just another gap in the minister's credibility?
There is no money for the provinces of Canada, no money for development of the

The Budget-Mr. Schumacher nation's human and natural resources, no money for fighting regional disparity or attacking unemployment and underemployment. There is no money for any of these vital undertakings but lots of money for federal ministers' housekeeping expenses.
When the government was busy cutting and hacking at potentially productive programs, why was no mention made of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? To my mind this is one of the greatest sink-holes in the whole fabric of the government of Canada. It is a drain down which tax dollars pour unchecked, uncontrolled, and apparently uncontrollable. costs each and every Canadian almost $8 per year. Its estimated expenditures this year are in excess of $151 million. And this does not include a $25 million "loan" for capital purposes.
The fact that the C.B.C. is a part of the government and nominally must report to parliament is the chief reason, I believe, why it is uncontrolled and uncontrollable. As long as it is connected with government, its defenders, the pseudo-intellectuals and bleeding hearts of all parties, will be able to come to its rescue whenever it is criticized by crying "politics". This is an absurd argument but one that is difficult to offset. By making the C.B.C. something sacrosanct and untouchable we have permitted the setting up within it of autonomous enclaves, little principalities running their own show, acknowledging no other authority than their own and living off the abundant flow of tax dollars ensured by a helpless government.
As a new member of this house, Mr. Speaker, it is amazing to me that the government has never deigned to recognize, let alone act upon, the strictures laid upon the C.B.C. by the nation's Auditor General, Mr. Maxwell Henderson. The Auditor General has pointed out that on the eve of the retirement of one of its vice-presidents the directors increased his salary by 67 per cent to $25,000 so that he could receive a pension equivalent to that of our former prime ministers, and then gave him a retiring allowance of $25,000. This is what the Auditor General said of this generosity with the taxpayers' money:
This was not within the competence of the directors of the C.B.C. and payment of the retiring allowance was not within the powers of the corporation under the Broadcasting Act.
The Auditor General said, in other words, that the C.B.C. authorized and paid out large sums of tax dollars without justification, and illegally. To add insult to injury the C.B.C., in spite of these comments by the Auditor General, subsequently proceeded to give equally generous pensions to other top C.B.C. executives. Was anything ever done by the government? No. Did the man who now weeps for scarce tax revenue shed a tear for such unjustified and wasteful use of public funds? No.
November 12, 1968

As Patrick Nicholson wrote at the time of Mr. Henderson's report:
The C.B.C., as has been made obvious over the years, has inflated itself into a self-governing empire beyond the control of parliament-and the government does nothing to stop it.
This is a pretty accurate summation of the situation as far as I can see. The fact is that the C.B.C. is a law unto itself. Government agents inserted into its structure, even at the top, are merely ignored or absorbed. A final measure of the C.B.C.'s arrogant self-assurance may be seen in the fact that in all the flurry of cancellations of projects in the sweet name of economy, not a finger was laid on the C.B.C. Its plush new office-studio complex of 23 storeys in Montreal will go ahead anyway, at a cost of $66 million. If it turns out like the National Arts Centre we could be running into a $300 million or $400 million project.
Until the minister and his colleagues can find some way to stop up the open sewers in their bureaucracy down which tax dollars are disappearing at an ever-increasing rate, it is a mockery for him to call for self-restraint and self-discipline in spending. These untouchable government agencies are only one of several areas of uncontrolled expenditure that make it impossible for any accurate forecasts to be made or to run the country on responsible fiscal principles.
The other most important area has already been dealt with at length by my colleagues in the opposition. That is the area of shared-cost, open-ended, federal-provincial programs. I will not deal with them now beyond saying that they are bleeding the country white, and the reason is simple. For purely political purposes federal Liberal governments of the past five years have concocted these programs too hastily, forced them upon provincial governments in no position economically or politically to oppose them and have failed, in setting up these programs, to provide any controls whatsoever upon expenditures. It is an example of negligence and irresponsibility without parallel, and to persist in the imposition of national medicare while at the same time announcing the intention to withdraw from the scheme in five years is, to say the least, amazing.
Before I close, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about another area in which I conceive this budget to be particularly weak. This is its failure to give any recognition to the basic economic development which must be the forerunner and foundation of any significant social development. This budget
The Budget-Mr. Schumacher makes much of the so-called social development tax. In my view this is simply a cheap method of camouflaging a straightforward, old-fashioned tax gouge.

I come from a part of the country that has more than a passing interest in wheat. It would be no overstatement were I to say that the social development of my area depends primarily on wheat. Foremost in the economic development programs of most urgency in my area is the development of a modern, efficient and effective sales and marketing set-up for wheat. Many speakers in many debates in this house have set out in detail just what a large and important part wheat plays in the Canadian economy and what a direct and important bearing it has on the well-being of many thousands of Canadians far from the wheat fields and 'the elevators. I will not go over that ground beyond quoting briefly from an address made only last month in Winnipeg by Mr. A. M. Runciman, president of United Grain Growers Limited. He said at one point:
Wheat growers have a legitimate right to ask for some sacrifice on the part of the taxpayers to maintain Canada's great industry of growing wheat for export.
Mr. Runciman also said that wheat growers had their responsibilities to the taxpayers too. One of the chief of these I believe is to ensure that the industry of producing wheat is not allowed to degenerate into a make work business, sustained only by generous transfusions of tax dollars from time to time in the form of subsidies or other artificial stimulants.
If we are to demand support from the body of the Canadian taxpayers we must ensure that wheat production remains a vital, necessary and lucrative business. This much is demanded by the national interest. If we accept this responsibility, however, as wheat producers we surely have a right to ask that the government assistance that is essential under our existing laws in support of the sale and marketing of wheat be the most modern, progressive and effective that it is possible for us to devise.
It is exactly in this area that 1 wish the Minister of Finance, and indeed the whole government, had shown some awareness of the vital necessity of moving swiftly and aggressively in the field of wheat marketing. I have no wish to burden the house with a detailed discussion of the complexities of wheat production, sale and distribution in
2642	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Marcel Lessard today's world market. It will suffice for me to quote Mr. Runciman once again. He said:
It is doubtful if exports this year will go over the 350 million bushels.
This, in a nutshell, is our problem-declining export sales in a world market where old, traditional customers are becoming less and less dependent upon us, new customers are ultra price conscious, and competition and production have gone up sharply.
One of the chief competitive factors we face in Canada is the greater flexibility our competitors enjoy in pricing to make sales. Our present set-up, which has served well and profitably over many years, has become a handicap in the changed circumstances of the world wheat marketplace. Valuable as may be a national grains council, I do not think the pressing facts of Canada's economic life, and particularly the pressing facts of western Canadian economic life, permit us the luxury of waiting until such a necessarily cumbersome body gets down to work. I would suggest that what we need is an immediate and massive attack on the twin problems of pricing our wheat for sale in competition with other producing nations and a determined and businesslike approach to the question of surveying new markets, encouraging new uses of grains, and making new friends, customers and sales.
It is not enough any more to depend on detached, long range sales techniques. In today's world wheat users will not come banging on our door. We must bang on theirs, but in doing so we must be sure we have the goods they want to buy. Wheat sales made at a ministerial or ambassadorial level can no longer be depended upon. Special trade missions with limited life and scope will not serve. We want special, expert, highly skilled and knowledgeable teams of Canadian traders on the job abroad 52 weeks of every year. We must have sales teams, market survey teams, promoters and idea men on this export job the year round, day in and day out. And behind them we must place the support of a very much stepped up agricultural research effort. We have to be aggressive. We have to go where the business is; we have to revolutionize our whole concept of selling wheat.
This, Mr. Speaker, is the sort of economic development which I believe should have been encouraged by this budget. This is the sort of concept the Minister of Finance might find much more productive of tax dollars than his present theories of regressive,

inward looking and outmoded national financing. This failure to arouse the spirit of the country, this failure to meet the real needs of Canada at this time, and this abject surrender to a gloom and doom philosophy I believe stand as the great indictment of this budget.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rising for the first time in this 28th parliament, after an absence of three years, I would like, before making remarks on the budget and the economy in general, to congratulate you for the confidence which the members unanimously showed you by electing you as Speaker of the house.
Having had the privilege of coming to this house at the same time as our Speaker in 1962, I have had the advantage of meeting him, and I was not at all surprised that he rose rapidly to the responsible position he now occupies with tact and competence.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I lived through the difficult years which this parliament experienced from 1962 to 1965, and I know that the 1965-68 period was just as difficult.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Indeed, during three and a half years, I took part in the debates many times, putting forward solutions and giving my opinions on the problems facing our country, and my area in particular.
Defeated as an independent candidate during the 1965 election, I accepted to be a member of the new Liberal team during the election of June 25 last, when the Canadian people gave this government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a clear mandate.
However, nobody expects miracles. Nowadays, every country in the world is going through difficult periods, and Canada as well. However, it is largely with us, members of this house, that rests the responsibility of deciding policies likely to provide all Canadians with one of the highest standards of living in the world.
Mr. Speaker, since I came back to this house, I have been happy to see that the atmosphere of the discussions has changed noticeably and that, in general, all hon.
November 12, 1968

members seem ready to co-operate in the best interest of Canadians. I think that this attitude of hon. members is due to the fact that more than a hundred of them are newcomers to the house and are interested in seeing this parliament progress as quickly as possible. I think it is the will of the great majority.
Personally, I agreed to come back to politics because I am confident that a renewed Liberal party, led by a dynamic and able young man, will find the new formulas needed to push our economy toward new heights.
The young people of Canada have also put all their hopes in that man and in this parliament, because to them the stakes are much more important; in fact, their future is at stake.
During the last few years, an always increasing number of students have reached the university level or have gone beyond the high school level. We have told them in the past that they would be successful if they continued their studies and became qualified. We led them to believe, and with good reason, that education was one of the conditions that would guarantee their future success.
In view of the technological changes which we have experienced in the last few years and which will increase in the years to come, I feel that we have not misled them by encouraging them to stay in school to acquire as much knowledge and as much competence as possible.
But today, Mr. Speaker, the problem which is facing us and which we must solve is that of an economy which is at a standstill and does not offer the job opportunities that those able young people trained in our schools are entitled to expect on the labour market. That is the tragedy, I think, that is the most serious problem and the great challenge we must face.
Personally, I cannot resign myself to seeing the young people back home expatriate themselves in order to earn a living. For too long now, we have seen that policy of inaction on the part of our administrators who banked on private enterprise and its good will. Far be it from me to blame private enterprise for that state of affairs. But this fact must still be recognized: in the past, our governments have relied on the more or less arbitrary decisions of private enterprise for the development of our economy.
But these times are gone and, today, it is the duty of the leaders of our country to intervene and to create the political climate
29180-167J
The Budget-Mr. Marcel Lessard and such conditions as will allow enterprises to be born and to flourish.
If we want to create an atmosphere propitious to the development of such undertakings and the economic progress of our country, the budgetary deficits Canada has known in the last ten years must come to an end. There is nothing worse then accumulated deficits, for they are the direct cause of the high cost of living, the increase in interest rates, in direct and indirect taxes and all the various taxes imposed upon the Canadian taxpayers.
It is our duty to return to the balanced budget, because no enterprise whatsoever can function properly when it anticipates on the income of future decades. In my opinion, the Canadian government cannot do better than private enterprise. Like Canadians themselves, it has limits to its spending capacity.
After discussing the matter with my fellow citizens, I have reached the conclusion that, for some years, the government should revert to the pay as you go policy. It should not incur expenditures which cannot reasonably be met through existing taxation and, if possible, taxation should be reduced. The present taxation system is detrimental to savings for all practical purposes. This inflationary period we have gone through is a reason why a man saving a dollar today will lose money tomorrow as this same dollar will have less purchasing power. In fact, I would say that, in its present condition, inflation encourages indebtedness. A man can today obtain more through borrowing than by waiting until later to buy what he wants with his savings. This is leading us into a disastrous situation. It will affect the family budget as well as the municipalities, school boards and the provincial and federal governments.
We must revert to a balanced budget, but we should not start by computing the expenses first and then obtaining revenues. In my estimation, a balanced budget consists in calculating first how it will be possible to obtain revenues through the existing taxes which the taxpayers can afford and the economy's producing capacity. On the basis of a probable and sufficient secure revenue, it must first be established in what fields the money is to be expended in order to stimulate our economy and our industrial development so that Canadians will be assured of some social security. However, our first objective must then take into account our economic development, because employment can create more income for the workers and they, in turn, are better able to look after their own social security.

The Budget-Mr. Marcel Lessard
I would like at this point, Mr. Speaker, to quote a statement made by the newly elected American president who, soon after his victory, said as reported on November 7 in Le Devoir:

In my opinion, in Canada, we have to restore a climate and an economic situation which will allow our industries to compete on foreign markets. If the formulation of this policy is considered in the United States, it should, all the more, be considered in Canada. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) suggests that we go back to a balanced budget system and I fully agree with him on that. However, I would make a reservation with regard to the increase in the budget itself, because if we compare it with the budget of six years ago, we find that to all practical purposes, it has almost doubled.
I do not think that this is something we should be proud of because, as was so well put lately by the honourable member for British Columbia, strong governments are not necessarily good governments.
I think we should avoid over-expansion, particularly here in Canada. In my opinion, the economy has produced enough money during that period of time to balance the budget, but our successive governments have imposed a great many new taxes and raised existing taxes. This policy should be abandoned.
The government and the various ministers responsible for the estimates should keep within the sums allocated to them. In my opinion, the ability of a minister-and I think that should be one of the most important criteria for judging the competence of a minister-is not necessarily proportionate to the importance of the budget he administers or the number of employees working under him. The riding of Lac-Saint-Jean is situated in the beautiful region of the Saguenay and lake Saint-Jean, some 150 miles north of Quebec city.
It is a somewhat isolated area, a valley which one discovers after travelling along a magnificent highway which cuts across the Parc des Laurentides. This area, Mr. Speaker, has a population of 280,000, and its economy depends mostly on agriculture, the pulp and paper industry and the production of aluminum.
During the past 25 and I would even say 50 years, our region has developed a great deal but now, as is the case with several other parts of the country, we are merely marking time for our industries are not developing and, since we depend almost completely on primary industries, we have almost no secondary industries. Unemployment has reached a rather alarming level.
At the present time, according to the statistics of the National Employment Service and Manpower Centre of our area, more than 15 per cent of the manpower is unemployed and must rely on unemployment insurance benefits and various welfare measures to make both ends meet. Mr. Speaker, such conditions cannot go on and should not be allowed. We should do everything possible to cope with it.
The milk industry is the main occupation of the farmers in my constituency. They are grouped in a recognized professional association which is well structured. For a great number of years, it has fought for the interests of regional agricultural class. The Catholic Farmers Union, to which belong most of the farmers in my district, has, during past years, worked tremendously hard to promote the interests of the agriculutral class.
Farmers now have organizations that are able to represent them well and especially to provide them with the necessary technical information to permit them to operate their farms with the greatest possible efficiency.
Mr. Speaker, for some years now, the Catholic Farmers Union through briefs has been asking for the establishment of an agricultural marketing board.
I realize, of course, the difficulty of establishing a set-up of that kind, but those farmers are aware nowadays of the fact that in
November 12, 1968

order to be successful, to obtain some kind of security, to be able to share the well-being of the rest of the Canadian people, they must surely be more efficient and get a better income for their work as well as better prices for their products.
I therefore ask the government to co-operate with the above-mentioned organizations in order to set up as soon as possible the agricultural marketing board, so that we may once and for all find a solution to the farmers' problems.
Mr. Speaker, in the Saguenay-Lac-St-Jean area-as everywhere else in Canada-we were pleased to hear that the people in Gaspe would at long last know a period of prosperity thanks to the application of a huge development program costing some $258 million.
In the last election campaign, the right hon. Prime Minister of Canada, and several of his cabinet colleagues, pledged themselves to work hard towards eliminating regional disparities. The Saguenay-Lac-St-Jean region is now experiencing difficulties and I feel that with its tremendous potential it is certainly the ideal area for an experimental project in development.
That is why, in line with my commitments during the last election campaign and with the support of the ministers, and especially that of the Prime Minister, we ask that some body be set up and some study be made and some program be established, taking into account, of course, our potential and our needs.
I feel that the people deserve that the government take care of them, as we have even now the qualified people needed to make a success of such an undertaking.
We are not asking for charity, but merely that we get back part of the taxes that we and our large industries, such as Alcan, have paid to the federal treasury in the past, and are still paying for that matter. If that money, or part of it, were reinvested in the development of our area, not only could we cease to depend on the help of the various governments, but we could then generate new income for the government.
Mr. Speaker, I could not resume my seat without having pointed out one of the serious problems which industry in general must now face because of recent discoveries, which I feel is becoming an increasing challenge to man, I am thinking of the progress of technology, mechanical engineering and automation.
The Budget

Mr. Marcel Lessard
Throughout the ages, the methods used to produce various consumer goods have changed. However, our generation is witnessing a unique phenomenon in the history of humanity, namely the rapidity with which those technological changes are applied in industry. Their introduction in industry has changed the methods of production. If they want to survive and prosper our industries have no choice; they must adapt their methods of production to the exigencies of national and international competition. For enterprises, mechanization is not a luxury; it is a condition of survival. Those which refuse to modernize, to fall into step, are simply doomed to disappear.
Mr. Speaker, during the next five minutes, I would like to mention one of the problems raised by the application of changes in factories. Their effect is to modify greatly the traditional way of producing and, therefore, workers are greatly affected. The displaced worker must go through job retraining. Quite often he finds himself out on the street without any job or income and completely lost.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
In a situation of this kind, a deep feeling of insecurity takes hold of the workers who will soon become the victims of our development. The present situation is all the more serious because the great majority of all industrial workers of this generation have been unable to take advantage of advanced academic training. For them, retraining is difficult, even impossible in some cases.
Confronted with the threat of mechanization and automation, the workers' unions have to fight progress, because they have no other alternative, especially when the unemployment rate is as high as it is today. Collective bargaining has become more and more difficult because, in addition to trying to improve working conditions and wages for the workers, the union leaders are compelled to fight dismissals resulting from technological changes.
Mr. Speaker, what is our responsibility as legislators in view of this situation? What have we done in the past? Very little, if anything. What does this government intend to do? I direct this question to the Minister of Labour, the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey). I do not know.
Since I have returned to the house, most of the members who have taken part in this debate have not said anything on this subject.
2646	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Marcel Lessard I am surprised at that and concerned, because after listening to all the members' speeches and finding that nobody was raising the problem of technological changes that affect the workers, I am wondering if we are not on the point of forgetting that we have been sent here by the great majority of workers. Workers are nonetheless affected by these changes and most of them are responsible for our being here. When the time comes to send them the bill of our budget extravagances, generally there is no delay. We have some more evidence of that.
As administrators of the business of the nation, our first responsibility is to foresee. We have only to recall the numerous strikes in public services to realize that we did not benefit from the experience of private enterprise in the field of collective bargaining. We have granted the right to strike to public servants without making sure, beforehand, that effective and approved machinery would favour the signing of conventions without numerous strikes.
To get out of this mess, we have been forced to grant wage increases that started the whole inflationary process, at the expense of all, and mostly of our industries which have been in an unfavourable position with regard to international competition.
Here, in Ottawa, when there are problems, we proceed with royal commissions of inquiry. That is not necessarily bad, Mr. Speaker. But while we investigate and conduct studies, there are some who suffer from the fact that we are doing nothing. When the commissions present their reports-and normally they do-what happens to them? Most often, some officials take a look at them, a few newspapers print excerpts, but unfortunately, very often, the reports lie on the shelves or they rot in the files where nobody reads them.
In the field of labour relations, the Freedman commission reviewed the situation resulting from technological and operational changes in the Canad'an National services. This report was published some time ago, but has anything been done about it? What plans are contemplated in order to implement the recommendations made by that commission?
There are several recommendations, Mr. Speaker, embodied in that report. One deals with the introduction of technological changes and if it were implemented through appropriate legislation, it might have a great impact on future collective bargaining.

DEBATES	November 12, 1968
In fact, Mr. Speaker, it is recommended by the Freedman commission that any technological change introduced during the life of a collective agreement should be subject to bargaining and that the workers could even go on strike if no satisfactory agreement is reached. Mr. Speaker the Freedman commission goes farther than that and this is very important.
It is recommended that those workers losing their jobs be compensated for their moving expenses, for the possible losses they sometimes incur and for selling their properties. It is even suggested that municipalities be compensated for the problems resulting from loss of revenues due to reductions in the number of employees or because of shutdowns by industry.
Mr. Speaker, if those recommendations are applied, they will have may implications. It will not be easy to make the companies understand this, and neither will it be easy to make the labour unions accept the regulations. However, I think it is our duty to tackle this problem and to find a solution to the application of modern technology which penalizes the workers for a time. It is indeed today's tragedy that the breadwinner lives with the impending menace of losing his job and his means of subsistence. I believe that is our primary responsibility.
I definitely intend to come back to this point because, as a worker coming from a working class family, I cannot dissociate myself from the problems of my fellow-Canadi-ans, my fellow-citizens, my colleagues and my friends. One of the questions I was asked very frequently during the last election campaign was: "What do you intend to do to protect us against automation?"
I think workers can be protected through legislation, but they can also and above all be protected by a flourishing economy which will increase the number of jobs available. Technological progress would present no great problems, Mr. Speaker, if there were many jobs available, because then, simply on account of the departure rate, the mortality rate and the retirement rate, companies could introduce new techniques, new methods of works and new machines without great prejudice to the worker. But unfortunately this is not the case. At present, the workers have no alternative. They are being laid off and there are no jobs available. If there were, I would be the first to ask for an immediate application of technological changes, as this
November 12, 1968

would, in the end, result in an economy of efforts, which is not the case now.
As this is not the case, we must find means of protecting the workers. Before I finish my remarks, I ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen), the two most involved here, to combine their efforts and bring this house to pass legislation as soon as possible to protect the workers' interests and insure full employment security for them and protection for their families.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ambrose Hubert Peddle (Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the rules of this debate are somewhat elastic and I hope you will pardon me if I tend to test their elasticity. From the way our so-called reformers are debating overtime it may be some time before I shall have another opportunity to speak.
I want to talk about the time just before this government took office. For a few months before that time a mania was rampant in this country. That is what the press called it. That term did not emanate from this side of the house. Please bear in mind that it originated with an approving press, a favourable press, sometimes, one might say, an adoring press. They called it "Trudeaumania". For the fun of it I brought with me a little dictionary of synonyms and antonyms and looked up the different meanings of "mania". The different shades of meaning listed are: madness, insanity, furore, adoration, amentia, dementia, morosis, frenzy, delirium, delusion, hallucination, and brainstorm.
I shall begin, as a foundation for my remarks, by saying that this is a very shocking basis for any government. On June 25 the people of Canada were subjected to a test, to an examination, if you wish, to see just how seriously they were infected by this mania. Sir, the results of that test confirmed our very worst fears. It had indeed reached epidemic proportions, serious but not incurable in the west, serious in central Canada, possibly incurable or possibly not; I don't know. But in the east the mania did not get off the ground because we in the east had developed an immunity to manias. We in Newfoundland in particular had developed an immunity to manias. We have been suffering from a very serious case of Joey mania for the last 20 years but I am proud to report to this house
The Budget-Mr. Peddle that recovery is on the way. In any event, we in the east did not suffer from this mania.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I am going to make a few observations now and I will try not to be too much of an isolationist or too parochial. I also hope to make a few remarks with reference to the national scene which may be regarded as pragmatic because many Newfoundlanders are inclined to see all black or white and very little grey. However, I was elected by the people to come here and say what I think and not what somebody else thinks.
I refer first to a colourful magazine that came to my desk today, "Montreal 68". I have been receiving it for some time and it is very interesting. It has an item headed "Montreal's Gift To Canada." For the benefit of the house, and I am sure not too many people are familiar with this, the article reveals that the full name of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is Joseph Philippe Pierre Yves Elliott Trudeau and that he was born in 1919, which makes him 49 instead of 46. But that is beside the point, Mr. Speaker.
I now wish to quote from a week end newspaper which states that the Prime Minister addressed some "3,200 smartly dressed people" who turned up at a $50 a plate dinner in the grand ballroom of a downtown Montreal hotel. I have no doubt that they did turn up smartly dressed and enjoyed their $50 a plate dinner.
The tenor of the Prime Minister's remarks seemed to revolve around political participation in democracy. This seemed to be the whole gist of his speech. He is worried about people not participating in politics in Canada.
I would like to point out that I have been a member of this house since September 12 and on only one occasion have I seen the Prime Minister sit in his seat and listen to the remarks of members of parliament. That one occasion was the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in the debate on the throne speech. As the Prime Minister is known to be the author of the throne speech, naturally common courtesy compelled him to be here on that occasion, but on not one other single occasion have I seen the Prime Minister remain in the house after the question period.
He goes about this country and talks about participating in politics. I would like to point out that we have a participatory form of politics. The people of Canada elected 264 members to come to this house. This is the way they participate. I suggest that the Prime
2648	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Peddle Minister sit in his seat and participate once in a while.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not worried because he is not here to hear my speech, but he is not even here to hear his own members speak. I am worried that this Prime Minister, who has been involved in Canadian politics only for the past two years, appears to know all the answers. But he gets up and with his ministerial following behind him he leaves, as though something dirty was going to happen here following the question period. He does not want to listen to the elected representatives of the Canadian people discuss their problems. He would rather go to a $50 a plate dinner in Montreal and invite the people there to participate in democracy. I suggest that the Prime Minister of this country sit in this house once in a while and listen to the representatives of the people. I suggest that when he rises from his seat and, with the ministers whom he permits to be here on a particular day, leaves the house, he is showing in no uncertain terms his contempt for parliament, his contempt for the 264 members who sit here, and his contempt for the Canadian people.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where is your leader?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And I see no reason in the world why he cannot test our present system of democracy which has been well tried. Our parliamentary system was not founded yesterday. When I entered the Newfoundland legislature for the first time some five or six years ago I confess that for the first six or seven weeks I said to myself, "This is a lot of garbage." But I soon found the reasons behind it. I soon found out, I soon learned and I soon appreciated why things were dragged out. We were members of the opposition and we were overpowered by a government that brought in legislation. But I could see that we were given the opportunity to question the legislation, to pick it apart, to examine it in detail. The system also gave the government the opportunity to stand behind its legislation and justify it.
Now the Prime Minister suggests that we speed up the parliamentary process, that we computerize it. According to the newspaper report he said:
In this age of computers and instant communications, parliament can no longer proceed with its traditional slowness-

DEBATES	November 12, 1968
He is impatient.
-without running the risk of always being left behind by advances in the life of society.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He wants to computerize all of us.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Maybe the Prime Minister would like to see 264 computers in the chamber. Maybe he would like to press buttons. Maybe he would like to become a benevolent dictator. This is what this statement suggests to me. He is worried because the Canadian people cannot participate in democracy. This House of Commons is the bulwark of democracy because here democracy is practised in this country. We do not want the Prime Minister, who came to power on a kind of a wave, a mania as the newspaper people described it, to come here and chip away at the bulwarks of our democracy. Let us reform parliament, Mr. Speaker, but I suggest that the Prime Minister is out to deform parliament, to destroy it. I quote again from the newspaper:
He called upon the people "to let parliament know they don't want this kind of delay"-
On June 25 the people of Canada knew what they were doing.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Or did they?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, that is not the question, but they did elect 264 members to this parliament under our present system. They were not anticipating any fancy system that the Prime Minister might come up with later. This is the system under which they elected us. This is the system under which we must serve until somebody comes up with a better system, and I am not at all convinced that the Prime Minister has a better system.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The Prime Minister suggests that he knows all the answers. I suggest he does not know the questions, let alone the answers. He says he expects to have a series of these $50 a plate dinners like he had in Montreal on Sunday night. I have news for him; he will have very few $50 a plate dinners in Newfoundland. This is all very fine, but the Prime Minister cannot wait until the end of the question period to get out of here. There would seem to be something unclean about this place. He must get upstairs, downstairs, or wherever it is, to closet himself with those pseudo-intellectuals, not the Canadian people, at whom he can crook his finger and say, "Come here, boy; I can use you." He wishes to further his
November 12, 1968



plans for some kind of a benevolent dictatorship or maybe one that is not so benevolent.
As I say, I am very concerned about this. It is all very well to be a member of the jet set. It is all very well to come swooping down in a jet, a helicopter, or what have you, speak to a group of people in a modern shopping plaza at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer in all probability, say a few well chosen words, give that famous smile, kiss a few teenage maidens, and take off again. I have figured out the reason the Prime Minister did not have much to say during his shopping plaza tours. He did not say much because he did not have anything to say. I have also figured out the reason for the famous haircut for which he is supposed to be responsible. It is not a hair style at all; it is only a very skilful attempt on the part of his barber to cover up his baldness. When the people of Canada realize this they may start to see through a lot more of these deficiencies.
The whole election campaign was won on two planks in the Prime Minister's platform. What were they? They were the just society and a promise to do everything that could be done about the regional disparity which exists in Canada. There is something else which has occurred to me. We have a new Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Bas-ford) who is very very concerned about this matter. He is the champion of the Canadian people. A few days ago he made a speech in the house in which he was very unctuous and pious. He mentioned that he is very much concerned about the wording of contracts, the fact that the weight of a product might be half an ounce less than it should be as marked on the container, and things like that.
I should like to talk about the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, this Canadian politician who goes back and forth across this country making irresponsible promises, the politician who stands up and suggests to the people of Canada that at seven o'clock in the morning on June 26 they will have a just society. I cannot help it if the people swallowed this; apparently they did. Now we learn that it will take time to bring all this about.
It is the job of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to see that the people of Canada are given the whole story. A few months ago the Prime Minister intimated to the Canadian people during the campaign that the Canadian economy was in wonderful shape. We know now that this was not true.
The Budget-Mr. Peddle Let us sick the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs on him because he misled the Canadian public. One is not supposed to do this. If we are not to have a just society that is founded on hypocrisy we must see that the Ministry of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is a real factor.
This department should be dealing with advertising, for instance in respect of cigarettes. It is recognized and accepted throughout the world that cigarette smoking can lead to lung cancer, another lung disease the name of which I do not know, heart disease, and a number of other diseases. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is very concerned about the fine print on finance contracts and about labels being correct; yet every time we sit down to look at television or open a magazine we see advertising that is designed to lure us into smoking a different kind of cigarette. We even learn that there is a new 12-minute cigarette that will give us lung cancer twice as fast as the compact 6-minute cigarette. All this goes on.
The minister is concerned about the fine print in contracts and the labels on packages, but these things will not give one lung cancer, emphysema or a heart attack. These are the things which receive the attention of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs while the cigarette manufacturers have a field day. They tell everybody down on the docks to smoke cigarettes. They show a big robust man with muscles. This will appeal to the younger generation. The suggestion is that you are a square if you do not smoke cigarettes.
This morning I saw a large billboard which said that everywhere today somebody is smoking a duMaurier. "Two pack Munro", as somebody said here the other day, says that smoking is declining for the first time since he became minister a few months ago. I am glad that he did not deliver the speech himself. He had his parliamentary secretary deliver it for him. I do not think he has any foundation for saying this, but it shows he is worried. What about the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro)? If his colleague the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs does not take action in this regard it is up to him to do something about it. Let us wipe out some of the newspaper and television advertising in respect of cigarettes. Incidentally, I should like to say to "two pack Munro" that I smoke two packs a day also.

You shouldn't.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As I say, there must be something done about this; otherwise we will be developing not a just society but a society of hypocrisy and a government of hypocrisy. If the government does not see its way to do something about this it will be the laughing stock of the Canadian people.
There is one other item I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Remember that on June 25 the people of Canada were sold a package. I suggest to members of this house that the package did not conform with the label indicating what was in the package. The label did not at all agree with what was inside the package. I refer to the practice of members of this present cabinet taking news releases of other members of the cabinet and rewriting them so they will be suitable for the consumption particularly of the voters of Newfoundland.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
I will not put the whole of this on record but I should like to refer to a news release by the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Marchand). It was released some time ago but the date does not really matter. He announced new mills to boost the Newfoundland lumbering industry. It is a very cautious and businesslike statement in which it is mentioned that this help to the Newfoundland industry would be conditional. The minister emphasized that these were normal public measures to aid in the development of a chip mill at Happy Valley, Labrador, and a liner board mill at Stephenville. He was very careful to emphasize that these were conditional but normal public measures. The minister was also very careful to say that some $6 million or $7 million of the entire $20 million would be recoverable from the companies, and that a large chunk of this, namely, the Atlantic Development Board portion, would only be payable after the companies became operative.
I suggest that at the very same time Newfoundland's representative in the cabinet of the government of Canada issued a release. What did he represent those measures as being? He represented them to the Newfoundland consumer as a great, magnanimous gift from a magnanimous government. He mentioned nothing about conditions and nothing about these amounts having to be repaid by the operating companies. He mentioned nothing apart from the fact that Newfoundland was to be the recipient of a $20 million
[Mr. Munro.J

gift from the government at Ottawa. We have a Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to protect the Canadian public against wrong labelling and so on, but who is going to protect the Canadian public from this type of misrepresentation which is just as serious as improper labelling?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who will protect the Minster of Defence Production (Mr. Jamieson) from the government?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let us have another minister to protect the people of Canada from irresponsible politicians.
I promised not to become insular or parochial, but before resuming my seat I should like to put a few words on record about regional disparity. Let me give the house an example of regional disparity of the type that should be labelled "made in Canada", by the government of this country. I refer to the installations and buildings maintained by the Department of National Defence in Canada. Very quickly I should like to give figures in relation to the total number of people, both military and civilian, employed in the provinces in this regard. In the province of Newfoundland there are 559; in the province of Prince Edward Island, there are 1,674; in the province of Nova Scotia there are 20,105; in the province of New Brunswick there are 7,612; in the province of Quebec there are 15, 227; in Ontario there are 42,071; in the province of Manitoba there are 8,785; in Saskatchewan there are 2,214; in Alberta there are 8,877; and in British Columbia there are 12,782. Surely this is regional disparity of a kind that should be labelled "made in Canada." Perhaps it should be stamped, "made in Canada by a government with obviously no concern about correcting it." Some attempt should be made to equalize defence spending across this country.
All sorts of things of a serious nature to the province of Newfoundland have taken place since this government took office. Let me refer to the salt rebate program. The Minister of Defence Production has belittled this program. He is an affluent man and knows nothing about poverty. He suggests this means only $50 or $60 to the fisherman. From very good advice I know that it means $170 or $180 to some of our fishermen, and twice as much or $340 when that man is fishing with his son. The minister has suggested this is band-aid treatment. I asked the doctor who shares my place here what one should do if one has a wound and only has a band-aid. I
November 12, 1968

asked whether one should pluck off the band-aid and let the victim bleed to death or leave it on until a better bandage was available. He replied that of course common sense would tell you to use whatever you had and make the best of it. He said we should not pluck away the band-aid in the way the Minister of Defence Production has suggested. His analogy there bears some examination.
I do not come here asking for handouts for the province of Newfoundland. We do not want silver platter treatment. Newfoundlanders do not want to be given a living but they rightfully feel they are entitled to the opportunity of earning a living. This is a responsibility of this government and I humbly suggest it should get going to find a solution, even at the expense of some of the other programs which cost millions of dollars.
Once the big problem of unemployment is solved the other problems will become smaller. I am sure that problems in respect of bilingualism will decrease. There is one common language in this country and that is the language of hunger. If you ask our unemployed, French speaking friends in Quebec what is more important to them, finding jobs or-
