subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great honour to rise in this house today to speak for the first time. It is also a great honour to be the first member of parliament for the new riding of Scarborough West. This riding was created in 1966 by the redistribution act, with the northern half carved out of the huge, old York-Scarborough riding and the southern half coming from the former riding of Danforth.
At this time I should like to pay tribute to the former members of parliament who served these two parts of my new riding recently, including Mr. Frank Enfield, Hon. Frank McGee, and Mr. Maurice Moreau, as well as the present member of the new riding of York-Scarborough (Mr. Stanbury). These members represented the old riding of York-Scarborough from 1953 to 1968. I should also like to pay tribute to Mr. Reid Scott, who represented the former Danforth riding from 1962 to 1968. While all these members did not belong to the Liberal party, they were all active and articulate members who served their constituents well, and it is a privilege
The Budget-Mr. Weatherhead
and a challenge for me to try to follow in their footsteps.
Scarborough West comprises the southwestern part of the borough of Scarborough, which is the most easterly of the six municipalities making up metropolitan Toronto. It runs for about five miles north from the Scarborough bluffs of Lake Ontario and it is about three miles wide. In this comparatively small area dwell about 85,000 people, still predominantly of Anglo-Saxon origin but being more and more enriched by peoples of almost all racial, cultural and linguistic origins. Until the end of the second great war much of the riding consisted of farm land, but in the ten years or so thereafter it became completely built up, mostly with single family houses but also with some parts devoted to a wide variety of light industry.
During the election campaign last spring I devoted considerable time, while canvassing door to door, attending coffee parties and public meetings, to discussing the desirability of a one Canada policy, not only to allow equal opportunities for our French and English speaking peoples right across the country but also economic opportunities. Every effort must be made to develop those parts of Canada which, because of conditions, have not been so fortunate, particularly the Atlantic provinces, parts of Quebec and other rural areas in Canada.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
While the great majority of my constituents are in the middle income bracket from which most of the taxes are raised to run this country, and while increasing living costs are pressing many of them quite severely, the people of Scarborough West are willing to concede that there are many parts of the country that need substantial, additional help, and they are willing to contribute to the worth-while and essential national goal of equality of opportunity no matter in what part of Canada one is born or lives. Therefore it is with much sympathy and some understanding that I have listened to hon. members in the house for the last two months relate in detail the problems particularly of the Atlantic provinces and some of the rural areas of this country.
I am sure that in the next few years our government, led by the initiatives of the new department of regional development, will add to and improve the many excellent regional development programs that we have started in recent years in order that this ideal of
2652	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Weatherhead equality of economic opportunity will rapidly become a reality. However, I trust that my hon. friends who represent these areas will also reciprocate this sympathy and understanding when we deal in this house with the problems of the great majority of the people of Canada, the problems of those who live in the urban areas of this country.
As is well known, about 70 per cent of all Canadians now reside in cities and within about ten years this figure will rise to about 80 per cent. Therefore in 1980 about four out of every five Canadians will not be in the outports of the Atlantic provinces or on the farms in the west but will be living in the great urban areas of Canada. Accordingly, now and to an ever-increasing extent in the near future, the problems of Canada will be the problems of Canadian cities. These problems are severe and their solutions are difficult and expensive.
However, if Canada is to prosper and remain a good place in which to live and raise a family, the problems of Canadian cities, in which most Canadians live, must be attended to and attended to quickly. Despite overlapping constitutional jurisdictions in some of the problem areas of pollution, transportation and housing, the federal government in my view must take a larger and more important role in dealing with these problems.
Of the various urban problems I would like at this time to say a few words with respect to housing. I was certainly pleased when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) appointed the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) as the minister in fact responsible for housing, because of his past personal experience in the housing industry in metropolitan Toronto, particularly in the Scarborough area, and because of the minister's reputation for getting difficult jobs done. I was also pleased when the task force on housing, under the direct leadership of the minister, was announced with a view to touring the country and getting the opinions of all interested and knowledgeable people and organizations with respect to this major national problem and reporting some concrete findings and proposals by early 1969.
As you may know, Mr. Speaker, a group of interested citizens and elected officials from all levels of government, school board, municipal, provincial and federal in the Scarborough area, including my good friend the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) and myself, discussed the problem

DEBATES	November 12, 1968
and then prepared a joint brief which we had the privilege of submitting to the task force at its hearings in Toronto last month. While our brief did not specifically mention this, I believe first of all that a new federal department of urban affairs should be created. Such a department would be able to be an effective liaison not only between the various federal departments interested in urban matters but would be able to direct and increase the cooperation among the federal, provincial and municipal levels of government, which is so necessary because of the overlapping constitutional jurisdictions in this field.
Such a new department would also be able to focus federal interest and concern on urban areas and also stimulate research, both in our universities and in the department itself, on urban problems. We have had departments of fisheries and agriculture ever since confederation and now, when most Canadians reside in our cities, I strongly submit that a department of urban affairs, with its own minister in the cabinet, is not only desirable but absolutely necessary.
Second, Mr. Speaker, it is apparent that there is no shortage of land for housing, even in an urban area like metropolitan Toronto. However, the cost of land has risen so sharply in recent years that a modest home is no longer possible. While speculation accounts for some of the increase, it seems that this was made possible by the shortage of serviced land available for development. Municipalities have found it difficult to finance the costs of services such as sewers and water mains, and they have resisted a too rapid growth in housing until sufficient industrial development has been attained to offset the costs of future services such as education.
While some of the possible financial solutions fall mainly in the provincial field, such as a possible equalization of assessment practices on land and buildings to discourage land speculation and the transfer of most educational costs from the municipalities to the provinces, the federal government still has a definite part to play. One way to reduce land costs and make land readily available for housing would be to encourage municipalities and regional governments to act as developers on their own through land acquisition. Federal loans at favourable interest rates might be provided for this purpose on condition that serviced lots were leased or turned over at cost after services had been installed. Although C.M.H.C. can now act in partnership with provincial authorities, our experience in Scarborough with the Malvern project
November 12, 1968
would not suggest that involving the provincial authority leads to quick solutions. The regional or municipal governments, on the other hand, with appropriate assistance from the federal government could probably act more quickly in conjunction with their own planning authorities, thereby eliminating an important source of conflict.
Third, in order to achieve the necessary increase in housing units across Canada from the level of 180,000 in 1968 to 225,000 by 1970, in accordance with needs as projected by the Economic Council of Canada, we will require an additional $1 billion each year in residential mortgage funds. Substantial new sums of money will also be required for public housing to assist families with low and modest incomes, retired people and students. Therefore, much of the additional funds for residential mortgages will have to come from the private sector, and in our brief to the task force some of the following ideas were suggested by which these funds could be generated.
(a)	Trust and loan companies could supply a substantially larger volume of funds to finance housing if present legislation were amended to allow them to borrow for terms exceeding the present limit of five years, in the same way as recent changes in the Bank Act permit chartered banks to borrow on subordinated, long term debentures.
(b)	Trust and loan companies registered under the federal government deposit insurance plan should be permitted to increase their borrowing ratios from 15 times paid-up capital and reserves to 20 times these reserves. This would enable them to increase borrowing capacity in the market by 33 per cent and would enable them to significantly increase lending on residential mortgages.
(c)	Pension funds are the most rapidly growing form of savings flow in Canada and have the greatest potential to contribute to the financing of new housing. However, in 1967 only 9 per cent of $8 billion in trusteed pension funds was invested in mortgages. If the pension funds were to increase by four times the proportion of their assets in residential mortgages, they would only equal the mortgage proportion in the portfolios of many life insurance companies. An active promotional program should be undertaken among pension managers to encourage mortgage investment, and the legislative requirements under which they operate should be thoroughly studied with a view to removing any technical or archaic impediments to their
The Budget-Mr. Weatherhead investing in greater amounts of residential mortgages.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
(d)	A secondary mortgage market should be established, with C.M.H.C. prepared to enter the market as a buyer as well as a seller. While C.M.H.C. should not be expected to guarantee the purchase of blocks of mortgages in the market in the absence of other buyers, any more than the Bank of Canada is obliged to support the Canada bond market under all conditions, a developmental approach on the part of C.M.H.C. to demonstrate a willingness to act as a seller or buyer in the interest of stabilizing prices would encourage the holding of larger mortgage portfolios by both small private investors and institutional investors concerned with liquidity.
Fourth, with respect to public housing, while the federal government supplies up to 90 per cent of the capital funds for public housing, up to 75 per cent for land assembly, and 50 per cent of the funds for subsidized rents in accordance with family incomes, the constitutional responsibilities for public housing lie largely with the provinces, and I would urge the federal government to take the lead in encouraging the provinces to create active housing authorities to make greater utilization of these programs right across the country. Although the quantity of public housing units immediately required is of paramount concern, we must be careful not to overlook the human aspects of the problem. If we continue to create apartment ghettos without providing recreational facilities, or without an appropriate dispersion throughout a somewhat mixed social and economic neighbourhood, or if we continue to treat public housing tenants as second class citizens, we can expect to find in a few years time that this great expenditure of public funds will have created serious social problems.
In particular, I would recommend using the present section of the National Housing Act which allows the spending of moneys by C.M.H.C. on ancillary matters appropriate to the project to encourage the installation of proper and sufficient recreational facilities in and about the larger public housing projects. The creation of proper public housing should be concerned not only with the bricks and mortar of the buildings themselves but also with the creation of the whole environment of living. Hopefully, it could be arranged to open such recreational facilities to the whole

2654	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Weatherhead surrounding community, but in any event I feel strongly that such facilities should be considered a necessary and integral part of any large public housing project.
While limited dividend housing has been subject to severe criticism, not the least in Scarborough, the program, given a sufficient supply of funds, could generate a major expansion quickly. Not the least consideration is the fact that though publicly assisted the housing is self-sufficient and particularly geared to families of moderate income.
Fifth, the lack of standardization on all building codes must be an important source of delay, red tape and added costs. Present building codes are too rigid and restricted, particularly in their response to new technology. C.M.H.C. should definitely take a much stronger lead in the standardization of regulations and products. Along this line it could encourage the use of new and cheaper materials and promote their acceptance by local authorities and building codes. It might also promote national standards in dimensions of windows, doors, etc., and it could test and promote the use of prefabricated modular units such as bathrooms, kitchen units and complete homes.
Lastly, rapid transit could play a major role in making additional land and satellite communities attractive for low cost housing. Adequate land for housing with convenient access to the city would tend to stabilize prices, rents and excessive speculation. The federal government's role in transportation in Canada's history is well established, with its support of railways, the trans-Canada highway, etc., and since the great preponderance of Canadians are now living in or very near to the big cities, subways and commuter rail services can no longer be considered as a purely sectional interest. Such rapid transit facilities must be built around regional planning in the use and development of land for housing, and the federal government, particularly through a new department of urban affairs, should closely co-operate with the provincial and regional authorities which constitutionally have the prime responsibility for such planning.
I see that my time is almost gone, Mr. Speaker, and I am sorry that I will be unable to comment directly on the budget in very great detail. In campaigning last spring I found that the people of Scarborough West were convinced that the present tax laws at all levels of government were inequitable and that substantial changes should be made to

DEBATES	November 12, 1968
make taxes fairer to all concerned. I certainly share this view and to me, therefore, the reform measures in the new budget with respect to the increased taxes on life insurance companies, on the banks and on the resource industries, as well as the exemption from estate tax of estates left to widows, are very welcome and are definitely steps in the right direction. However, more important is the definite assurance by the Minister of Finance that substantial new tax reform legislation will be introduced within the next six months.
I hope that among the tax reform proposals next spring some form of capital gains tax will be found. I am therefore looking forward with high expectations to the new tax reform legislation in general since to me its implementation will be one of the most important things this parliament will be doing over the next three or four years. While no one likes increased taxes, I believe the people of Scarborough West and the country realize that the new social development tax of $120, which decreases for those having taxable incomes of less than $6,000, is necessary as a contribution by each of us to the large sums of federal funds being spent on the very necessary and worthwhile social programs of hospital insurance, and to post-secondary education, and medicare. I am very proud of the lead the Liberal party has always taken in establishing nationwide social programs of this kind, and I believe the people realize that moneys have to be raised to pay for them. This new tax and the substantial increases in taxation of the insurance companies, banks and resource industries already mentioned will definitely allow us to work toward a balanced budget in the next fiscal year, which will provide a firm base from which substantial tax reform legislation can be introduced, debated and implemented.
Before concluding I would like to mention my high hopes for the proposals that the parliamentary committee for reforming the rules and procedures of the House of Commons will be presenting to us next month. As a brand new member I feel a little presumptuous in looking forward to changes in the rules when I am very aware that I do not fully understand the present ones. I also try not to advocate change just for the sake of change. However, times are changing more quickly than ever before and the people of the country expect, and I believe have a right to expect, that parliament will be able to amend its rules
November 12, 1968

and procedures in order that the great backlog of proposed legislation in all federal departments can be brought forward, debated, amended as necessary and passed as expeditiously as possible.
I realize and agree that the rights of the opposition parties to fully criticize proposed legislation and the estimates, etc., have to be protected, but I am sure that full and adequate protection can be given while at the same time changing substantially the present rules and procedures to speed up the flow of parliamentary business. Such reform is greatly desired and demanded by most Canadians and surely it is a basic prerequisite before parliament can hope to deal with all the problems and challenges of Canada as it enters its second century.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Scarborough-West (Mr. Weatherhead), on a very fine maiden speech and an excellent contribution to this debate. You know, visitors from other countries who have listened to the opposition speeches in recent days must retreat from this chamber in bewilderment and dismay. They must think to themselves, surely this is a paradox in paradise. When one listens to the opposition speeches, one must believe Canada is in dire ruin and unemployment is shockingly high; there is irresponsibility everywhere and disillusionment in the land. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, the case of the opposition has been so grossly overstated that it certainly is not going to influence the Canadian people. Almost without exception, these opposition speeches have been epistles of doom and disaster.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You should have heard the Liberals in 1960.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
These speeches lack the basic quality of optimism. If a Liberal were to refer to this glass of water he would say it is half full, but a Conservative or a New Democrat would say it is half empty. This is the difference in philosophy between these parties. There is a spirit of optimism which prevails in government ranks in this house. The Canadian people detected this difference between the parties and this is one of the basic reasons there is a Liberal government today while the other parties are in opposition.
The Budget-Mr. Perrault
I should like to refer to some of the facts relating to this budget. I should like to quote the remarks of some of the members of the opposition. On page 2262 of Hansard an hon. member is reported as saying there is a "lack of credibility" in the government. A prediction was made by one opposition member that the budget "will be a dismal failure". The prediction was made also that "hard times are ahead" and "there is a likelihood of tax increases". Then we had the prediction of "a deficit of alarming proportions". This can be found on page 2263 of Hansard. The budget critic of the New Democratic party said the budget was a "colossal fraud". Actually, these words are rather temperate in comparison with some other words which have been uttered during this debate. Then he said "the budget was unenterprising, unfair and a budget for the privileged". Suffice it to say that none of these members has ever been accused of being an optimist and, true to tradition, these are not optimistic remarks.
The fact is that during an extremely difficult time in the history of the world-a time of gold crisis, an international exchange crisis and monetary crises in a number of nations, Canada has weathered the storm remarkably well. These are the facts. At no time in the twentieth century has there been a more difficult economic storm for a Canadian government to weather. Yet this government has come through. And looking to the future, surely there are grounds for optimism-an optimism so lacking in the claims of the "gold dust twin" parties, representatives of which we have heard speaking in these past days.
We have seen exports increase in recent months. We have seen good support for consumer expenditures. We have seen sharp increases in tourist expenditures and we have seen a record number of housing starts. I had the opportunity of attending some of the housing task force hearings on the Pacific coast during the past week. I feel, as a result, it is most unfair for any opposition member to stand up and accuse the government of lack of action in the field of housing. I think it is most unfair, particularly in view of the excellent briefs which are being presented from coast to coast in this country. All parties should work together to support constructive action in the area of housing, especially for those lower income groups requiring special assistance.
As for the budget, you would think even members of the opposition would be able to raise a faint cheer for the 7 per cent increase
2656	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Perrault in gross national product in 1968. Even they should welcome the tact we are going to increase our real output in the neighbourhood of 3.5 per cent. This record is not as good as most of us would like, but it is progress; we are moving ahead.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Do not be too critical or pessimistic.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
All is not "lost". The situation is not "desperate". Compared with some other jurisdictions we are doing extremely well. We, in common with most nations, are battling the twin evils of inflation and unemployment. The programs which have been launched by this government should produce beneficial results in both areas. When we talk about inflation in Canada, let us not use the word too glibly and attempt to portray Canada as a nation where inflation has run away, where it is out of control.
I have taken the opportunity of checking some facts. Australia, Thailand, South Africa, Switzerland, Portugal, Ecuador, Austria, Ireland, Pakistan, Italy, The Philippines, Japan, Spain, Bolivia, Turkey, Peru, and many other nations one could name all experienced depreciation in the purchasing power of their currency in 1967. All of them are battling the same problem we are battling here in Canada. In most cases they are fighting a less successful battle than we are in our own nation.
Our friends in the New Democratic party have been lecturing us during the budget debate, as is their wont, on the need for social planning. Let us look at Scandinavia which is supposed to be the shrine of socialist endeavour. While Canada's currency suffered a depreciation rate of 3.4 per cent in 1967, the rate in Sweden was 4.1 per cent, Norway, 4.3 per cent, Denmark, 7.6 per cent and New Zealand, also cited by our friends in the New Democratic party, was 5.8 per cent. Between 1957 and 1967 Canada experienced an average annual rate of depreciation of its currency of 2 per cent, while the rate for Sweden was 3.7 per cent and for New Zealand 3 per cent. These facts are not cited to support inflation but they represent an attempt to put inflation in Canada in proper perspective in the world, something I suggest the opposition members should have done before they made some of their comments during this debate.
I do suggest that for the opposition to imply that Canada stands alone in some sort of inflationary crisis is palpable nonsense, and they know it is nonsense. If we can agree on

DEBATES	November 12, 1968
anything in this house it is that the government's efforts to battle inflation deserve the support of all parties. And in this fight against inflation the provinces must not opt out as "conscientious objectors" because there has been a vastly greater increase in provincial and municipal expenditures over the past ten years than there has been in the expenditures of the federal government.
Never have Canadians simultaneously sought national and individual freedoms on so wide and swift a scale and yet in the process set themselves on the brink of losing all freedoms by unleashing inflation. The opposition members in this house who suggest that the fight against inflation should be only a minor side skirmish are just as misguided as those who state that at all times and in all years the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has only one useful function and that is to balance the budget. Both of these concepts are wrong, destructive and ill advised.
The goals today, as they have been elucidated by the Minister of Finance, are these: full employment, a high rate of economic growth, reasonable stability of prices, a favourable balance of payments and an equitable distribution of rising incomes. It was a difficult task for the previous Conservative administration to achieve a proper melding of these objectives. It is a difficult task for the government here today, just as it is a difficult task for the provincial governments. No one should suggest that budgetary problems can be resolved by some basic, fundamental, simplistic action like merely proclaiming that a budget be balanced and then proceeding to do so. And those friends in the opposition who would vastly increase our social welfare programs regardless of inflation advocate, in effect, policies that would be disastrous for those in need. We have heard many proposals from the opposition side of the house suggesting limitless increases in benefits to various people. Not once, Mr. Speaker, has a price tag been put upon these programs, and I say that is not responsible opposition. Unless increases in Canada's human programs are funded in increased productivity and in meaningful purchasing power, then these programs are a fraud, a delusion, and would be ruinous especially to those who live in deprivation.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
During the recent campaign and during this session, Mr. Speaker, one clear message has issued from the government, and it is this: If we demand an increasing range of government supported services, then we must be
November 12, 19B8	COMMONS
prepared to produce more and to pay more; to assent to more taxes, if these services are to be provided on the basis of economic reality instead of economic fallacy.
There is a widespread misconception, Mr. Speaker, propagated by opposition parties in the house that some sort of fiscal and financial fourth dimension exists, a monetary fourth dimension from which claims for government support can be satisfied. There is no fourth dimension of this kind. Neither this government nor any other government can hand out more than what it has taken from others, be it by taxation, tolls, fees, duties, or by the insidious and appallingly unfair method of inflation, which is the taxing of those who have to restrict their spending because their incomes do not rise as fast as the value of money falls.
The Economic Council of Canada reminds us, Mr. Speaker, that we must create 1.2 million new jobs in Canada every five years. The challenge before us, regardless of our political affiliation, is to bake a bigger economic pie so that there will be new jobs for our young people coming on to the labour market, and new taxes and revenues in order to bring the just society to more Canadians.
Those people who have participated in this debate and have had nothing but words of criticism for the efforts of this government should refer to a survey conducted by the Organization for Economic Co-Operation and Development which was issued this year. They will not find the same critical tone in this objective analysis of the way Canada's affairs have been managed. I should like to quote an extract from page 31 of the report:
In the last two years, with the trend of business conditions changing quickly, the authorities have on the whole been successful in maintaining relatively high levels of employment while combating first excesses and then mildly recessionary tendencies appearing on the demand side. Both monetary and fiscal policies have been rather promptly adjusted to changing conditions.
This report is not a partisan one, Mr. Speaker. The Organization for Economic CoOperation and Development is a group set up in December, 1960, by the member countries of the Organization for European Economic Co-Operation and by Canada and the United States. Canada is held in high repute in international monetary and financial circles for the job we are doing in trying to restrict inflation as much as possible while at the same time maximizing employment opportunities. We have in this budget, something that reflects
DEBATES	2657
The Budget-Mr. Perrault admirably and well the government's intention to press on with this realistic approach to promote programs that at some later date will be productive of wealth for Canadians and our economy.
The opposition, Mr. Speaker, represents this approach as some sort of fiscal calamity. In fact, vast amounts of money are being invested in programs which will within the foreseeable future pay rich dividends to Canadians in economically viable new regions of our nation and provide all Canadians with higher incomes. In the case of aid for higher education, in financial terms alone there will be a return of almost 20 cent on our investment.
All we have heard during this debate from the members of the opposition, Mr. Speaker, is narrow, negative, tunnel-vision criticism of the sort that cannot see beyond the next 12 months. The other day the leader of the Conservative party stood up like some biblical prophet and lectured the government on how it had failed the Canadian people, on how it had deceived the Canadian people. When the leader of the Conservative party was premier of the province of Nova Scotia he grabbed federal money with both hands. He has never gone on record at a federal-provincial conference as telling the conference participants that no, they must refuse aid because this might cause an imbalance in the federal budget and that they should be concerned about the Canadian economy.
I ask you to listen to these figures, Mr. Speaker. The leader of the Conservative party, who the other day had nothing but condemnation for this budget, should remember that in the year 1961-62, during that heady period of Conservative rule, the province of Nova Scotia received $56 million by way of federal payments. In fiscal 1967-68, as a result mostly of Liberal legislation, that amount had gone up to $181,702,000. This is for the province of Nova Scotia alone. I hear no members of the house saying that this aid should not have been extended to the province. Surely it is time for governments at all levels to give due credit to other jurisdictions attempting to assist them achieve certain economic and social objectives. This is not being done, Mr. Speaker.
The fund for Atlantic development has never been criticized by the leader of the Conservative party because the province of Nova Scotia benefits from that fund. I should like to refer to the fifth annual economic
November 12, 1968

The Budget-Mr. Perrault council review, which shows that the province of Nova Scotia received from the Atlantic development fund a total of $52 million by the end of 1967. Mr. Speaker, as a British Columbian I am not standing here today declaring that there should not exist an Atlantic development fund, because this program is needed. But proper credit should be given to a federal government which has a deficit this year largely because of efforts to assist provincial governments like Nova Scotia. I suggest that it is easy to direct criticism at the federal government in a surface, narrow way.
If we examine the total contributions to the provinces, excluding tax rental agreements, we find that during the last year of Tory rule only $1.17 billion went to the provinces. This year, Mr. Speaker, $2.81 billion will go to the provinces. There, Mr. Speaker, is where you find a large part of the answer to why we have a deficit. Will one of the opposition members stand up before this budget debate has concluded and explicitly state which program should be cancelled in order to bring the budget into balance? Because this is where we separate the men from the boys, Mr. Speaker. These people who were ready to vote aye for medicare, for the Canada Assistance Plan and for the Atlantic development plan now stand up in righteous indignation and declare that the federal government is spending too much money.

Mr. Speaker, I have been listening with great interest to members who have neat, pat solutions to Canada's fiscal and monetary problems and I along with many others have been unimpressed. In those Tory days of which hon. members of the opposition have spoken so lovingly and nostalgically, on

a per capita basis the provinces received $63.45 in fiscal 1962-63. This year the provinces will receive contributions of $135.81 per capita. It was $63 per capita in Tory days, Mr. Speaker; it is $135 per capita today. Again, I would ask the members of the opposition to tell us which programs they would like to have cancelled in their respective provinces in order to bring this budget into balance? Now is the time to stand up. We have been listening for six days to nothing but criticism; we now want to know which programs they want to cancel in order to bring the budget into balance.
In terms of a percentage of the gross national product, Mr. Speaker, the latest available figures show that 4.15 per cent went to the provinces in 1967-68, which is a vast increase over the days when the Conservative government was in power in this country. That Tory government with such an appeal for our friends to my left devoted 17.93 per cent as a total contribution to the provinces as a percent of total federal budgetary expenditures, less tax rental payments. In the fiscal year 1968-69 that amount has zoomed to over 26 per cent of the total budgetary expenditures. These are facts which are just as readily available to members of the opposition as to government members.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member tells only half the story.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In efforts to hasten the establishment of the just society, in efforts to equalize economic opportunity, educational opportunity and an opportunity for a decent standard of health, Liberal governments have established steady and rapid growth in federal contributions to the provinces. The share of total federal budgetary expenditures represented by these contributions has nearly doubled during the seven year period ending in the current fiscal year 1968-69.
The Leader of the Opposition in this house should be among the first to give due credit to the federal government for what federal aid has meant to his home province. When we look at the budgetary estimates of his own province while he was premier it will be seen that his provincial budgetary errors in forecasting amounted at times to considerably more than the 4 per cent figure he describes as "irresponsible" when applied to the federal government. The last available budget from Nova Scotia indicates that over 50 per cent of that province's revenue derives from tax
November 12, 1968	COMMONS
sharing arrangements and other federal payments.
You know, Mr. Speaker, we often hear members of the New Democatic party in this house suggest, as someone suggested the other day, that it is unfair, unchristian, undemocratic and totally wrong that there should be so much unemployment in Canada. The last time the C.C.F.-New Democratic party was entrusted with governing any part of this nation was in 1961, in Saskatchewan. In 1961 I took the opportunity to visit Saskatchewan and I attended the Saskatchewan federation of labour convention. With the indulgence of the house may I be permitted to tell the house what the Saskatchewan federation of labour thought about the socialist panacea for unemployment. They said in their convention report:
So far, the government of Saskatchewan has neither obtained the action from the federal government needed to increase employment let alone to create full employment, nor has it in the alternative, requested the necessary legal authority with a view to creating badly needed jobs-
So far as we know nothing whatever has been done (by the CCF-NDP Saskatchewan government) in this connection, although the need for such a step has become extremely urgent-
Even in such a relatively straight-forward matter as the collection of data on the labour force, nothing is being done within the province of Saskatchewan. We still have to rely almost entirely on the inadequate information provided by the federal government.
That is what was happening in 1961. Perhaps between 1961 and 1968 the socialist party in this house has evolved a magic formula to solve unemployment, something it could not do in 17 years of government in Saskatchewan. If they have discovered the new formula they have been remarkably successful in keeping it a secret. The fact is that when given the responsibility of government, political parties often change their attitudes. That is because they are faced with hard economic problems and facts, the solutions to which are not simple of achievement.
We have heard a great deal of talk about the 2 per cent social development premium which is to be levied on all Canadians. The funds from this source will be directed toward improving the health of the Canadian people. I do not like increased taxes; nobody here does. The premium is $120 a year, and there is a premium reduction for those who earn less than $8,000 a year, give or take a few dollars. That is the way to describe it.
For the family man with two children who now pays $150 a year in medical care premiums, the premium will be something like $66
DEBATES	2659
The Budget-Mr. Perrault a year. What does he get for it? In the case of British Columbia, the man's premier gets $23 million back in medical care grants from the federal government this year and over $50 million in medical care grants next year. These are facts. The man with two children should receive a premium reduction of about $75 a year in his medical care premium if, in fact, his premier passes along the full benefits of the federal medical care grants. The man making $3,500 a year with two children will pay $16 extra in taxes and receive back $75 in medical care assistance from the federal government, again provided the premier of the province passes this money along. But that is not the story told by the opposition, who wish to portray the government as a group of steely-eyed, heartless individuals intent on one thing only, the destruction of the little man.
The fact is that members of the opposition, almost all of them, voted for medical care and for the Canada Assistance Plan. They understood even in their remote way the need which exists in Canada. But it is not becoming of them, Mr. Speaker, to attempt to attack and denigrate efforts by the government to finance these great social programs. Their motives are patently political. Yet this is what we have seen in this debate. It has been suggested by opposition members that the medical care premium is-and I use their word-"oppression". It is clear that millions of people throughout the world wish they were suffering from such "oppression". Millions would welcome a medical care plan like Canada's.
It is most encouraging to hear the Minister of Finance say that in 12 months further reforms in our taxation system will be introduced to make taxation in this country more equitable.
This is a good budget, a heartening budget, a realistic budget, which sets worth-while and attainable goals. It offers more than pie-crust promises impossible of fulfilment. Above all, it is an optimistic budget reflecting the optimism which resides on the government side of the house with respect to the future of this great country.
In their frustration the fainthearted in opposition may condemn this budget, but the Canadian people are able to discern where their best interests lie. They do not lie on the opposition side of this chamber. They lie with a government which has established clearly
November 12, 1968

The Budget-Mr. McCleave its priorities in order to build a strong foundation for the country through sound economic, fiscal and monetary policies-a government determined to strengthen national unity between our two founding races. These are the best possible guarantees that we shall see a just society in the years to come.

Mr. Speaker, just before the adjournment the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Per-rault) had read to us his continuing jeremiad against the opposition parties in this house. I do not mind the hon. member preaching for a call to a higher notch in the just society, but when he reads speeches continually

and it seems to be the same one we have heard on a couple of previous occasions-I wish his call for higher duty could be mixed in with some extemporaneous prayer.
As a simile the hon. member held up a glass which contained some water and said that a Liberal would call it a half full glass of water because a Liberal was an optimist, while we on the opposition side would call it half empty. Knowing the habits of the hon. gentlemen with whom the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour is now associated in this house, I think he got his simile badly mixed. What really should have happened is that the glass would have been held up empty, but we would have been told it was filled to the brim with the most delicious of water.
Sir, it was about the time that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was born that the Liberal Federation of Canada met in Ottawa and passed a resolution, part of which dealt with medicare. It may be of interest to the house that the seconder of that resolution is now probably our senior parliamentarian, Hon. A. W. Roebuck, who is a distinguished ornament in the other chamber. Now we are told by members of the government that having brought in medicare they are going to withdraw from it. I think their behavior here is likened very much to that of a frolicsome young bachelor who is able to talk a young lady into certain action, takes a look at the bouncing baby boy-

I could deal with the other so-called shared cost programs in the same way, but there are three or four of them involving ten provinces and it would take a somewhat lengthy period of time.
For the benefit of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) I would like to say one thing before I turn to the main burden of my remarks about housing. It is with respect to a situation which I think is now developing across Canada in the collection of our national revenues. For years I believe the tax collectors had blinded their eyes to the so-called common law situations, but now they are not allowing people to claim as dependants those who are living with them in a so-called common law union.
This has been brought to my attention in at least one case in my area. The man in question has supported this woman for about 25 years but is not married to her. Now he has suddenly been told that he cannot claim her as an exemption. This will cost him a sum of $200 out of his own pocket. He wrote a very graceful letter in which he asked the Department of National Revenue to assume the responsibility for the lady, and see if they could feed and house her on $200 a year. But the letter unfortunately-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question, because I am sure he would not want to give the impression of producing the wrong kind of information. I wonder if he realizes that in fact our income tax law has never recognized common law relationships. If they have been allowed it is because they have never been picked up. I also think it is very unfair.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for his generous remarks. I think I did indicate when I was drawing this case to his attention that it was a matter about which the tax people had suddenly become aware after a large number of years. In any event my friend's letter, in which he offered to consign the lady in question to the Department of National Revenue if they could feed and house her for $200 a year, apparently fell into the hands of the computer in the department,
November 12, 1968	COMMONS DEBATES
because he did not get much satisfaction in the reply. Now, knowing that the minister is aware of the situation, I hope we can expect happier news in that direction when the next budget is presented by the hon. gentleman.
Now, sir, I wish to make a few remarks about the housing situation. This morning when reading a letter to the editor in the New York Times I was struck by some of the phraseology in it dealing with the terrible housing conditions that exist in many parts of the world, but in this case in particular in New York City. The writer pointed out that the pathology of deprivation to use his expression, meant that many people would be so emotionally crippled in their outlook before they even reached the first school years that tney could not carry on either as successful students or become successful citizens, but would instead become a burden to the state for the rest of their lives. I suggest, sir, that this wastage of human resources almost from the cradle is something to which we have to give a lot more serious attention in this rich country of ours. I think it is one of our most important problems and, as I shall note later on, I think we should make a rallying cry from here, from every legislative body, every council and chamber, every ratepayers association in Canada, that housing is a fundamental right of every citizen.
But before I get to that may I read from two newspaper clippings, the first from the Montreal Gazette of September 16, 1968, headed, "Poverty, Misery Found Here," which states in part:
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Poverty in Montreal has grown at such a rapid rate in the last two decades that more than half of the city's population now suffers "intolerable financial conditions," a local welfare executive said yesterday.
G. Roland Hennessey, assistant executive director of the Federation of Catholic Charities, told a poverty conference at Loyola College that the gap between the haves and the have-nots is widening steadily.
"Deprivation increased statistically six per cent in the Montreal area between 1946 and 1966. In 1946, 27 per cent of the population was destitute. In 1966 the count was 33.3 per cent."
Mr. Hennessey said today 38 per cent live in poverty, privation and misery' and 50 per cent suffer unbearable financial hardships.
You might note that this story was almost buried on page 3 of one of our leading Canadian publications. Then from my own area there is a story back on page 5 of the Halifax Mail-Star for Wednesday, September 4, 1968, which reads as follows:
The Budget-Mr. McCleave
Low Rental Public Housing: $165 a month?
Low rental public housing at $165 a month? That figure is the break-even cost of Dartmouth's first public housing project.
Planning director M. E. Lloyd told city council last night the low rental housing units would actually rent at $65 per month. This, he said, represented a $100 deficit on each unit.
The relatively high cost, $17,809 per unit, of the 40-unit public housing project, failed to raise an eye-brow from Dartmouth aldermen when details of the proposal were outlined at last night's general meeting.
Then further on the same report notes there is a waiting list of 250 persons for the public housing in the city of Dartmouth. These are just two examples. They were not very commonly displayed either. Perhaps we are becoming apathetic about this; I do not know. However, I believe it is something with which we must deal. A few weeks ago a number of members of this house, my friend from Toronto Broadview, my friend from Vancouver-Kingsway, myself and the Minister of Transport-perhaps there were others who I may not have noticed-were at the Canadian conference on housing held in the city of Toronto. This was sponsored by the Canadian Welfare Council.
For several days we heard statistic after statistic and harsh fact after harsh fact poured upon us about the problems of poverty and how they affect the home environments of tens of thousands of Canadians. Many resolutions came forward from that housing conference, but I think three are worthy of being placed on the record of Hansard. I believe my friend from Broadview and my friend from Vancouver-Kingsway and myself claim some credit for the first one. In a political way we thought the conference could make its record more effective if it stated a simple declaration in its first paragraph concerning what should be the goal of Canada. Here it is, although not as we undoubtedly would have written it. However, this is the form in which it was written at the conference, and adopted:
The Canadian Conference on Housing (1968) declares that all Canadians have the right to be adequately housed, whether they can afford it or not.
Then I should like to read paragraphs 3 and 5 of the same report:
There should be greater freedom of choice of appropriate housing for low and middle income groups, choice with regard to location, design, and ownership (private, cooperative, non-profit, public).
Canadian housing goals will not be easy to achieve. They require much higher priority within the national economy and should be seen to be as
2662	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. McCleave socially essential as education. No government is spending according to the priorities this conference insists on.
To that I say, "amen". Well, the problem is here; it receives a certain amount of publicity. A dominion-provincial conference on housing was held earlier this year. The former minister of labour who is now the Lieutenant-Governor of the province of British Columbia went about Canada last year investigating the situation. He held meetings everywhere. Now the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) in his capacity as spokesman in this parliament for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is doing the same thing. However, I believe there are certain facts so obvious that any task force would fail to uproot anything new about them. There are certain hard steps which in the long run must be taken. Certainly the problem of land values demands an approach which probably is beyond the political philosophies of most of us. Yet these steps undoubtedly will have to be taken.
I think there are steps which should be taken now and which should have been taken at the time the budget was presented to us by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). What group does the housing problem hit? I suggest particularly those in the low income brackets. The richer person will not have to sleep out in the open or on a muddy floor. He will find some place to lay his head and will be able to pay the price for that accommodation. But there are people who live in dire poverty in urban and rural areas in every province of Canada. For them we must emphasize over and over again, until it becomes a cornerstone of our political tradition no matter what part of the house we are in, that something must be done to see that more public housing is provided in Canada. It is as simple as that. There is something else which I believe could be brought about by federal impetus. I have in mind the provision of minimum standards in respect of housing across Canada. In this regard national standards are a help to municipalities which cannot afford the necessary research. I believe the federal authority could play a very proper role in this regard.
In my own city of Halifax minimum standards have existed for a period of approximately ten years. This has done much to build up the older stock of housing and maintain it at reasonable and livable levels in the city in which I live. If I have any objection to the minimum standards it is that they should be upgraded at intervals. Every decade the

DEBATES	November 12, 1968
level should be raised another 10 per cent, let us say. In this way existing housing can be conserved. If the only approach to public housing should be that we have to pay up to $15,000 for an old home, tear it down and replace it with public housing so that the cost of every public housing unit in the development becomes somewhere in the order of $27,000 or $30,000, I dare say none of us in this chamber could go into a venture like that if we had to commit ourselves to an expenditure of that magnitude.
There is another step; that is, to get rid of the 12 per cent sales tax. I believe this is one of the most iniquitous taxes devised by revenue hungry people. Volume V of the report of the Carter royal commission on taxation deals with sales taxes, and at page 74 states:
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
On economic grounds, we believe, as we have already stated, that all goods and services used to produce or distribute goods and services for final use by individuals should be exempt from sales tax. To remove the regressive features of a sales tax we have argued that shelter should also be exempt from tax. There is, therefore, neither economic nor social justification for the taxation of building materials.
One of the effects of this sales tax is the inevitable and unfavourable increase it has on the cost of homes. The tax measure itself has to be administered by approximately 11,000 different organizations and companies across Canada which deal in building materials. They must employ extra staff or set aside time to look after these taxes. I know from personal experience, having dealt with some of these companies, that they have a terrible time in their dealings with the Department of National Revenue. This is not because the department has any idea about skinning them or making life miserable. It has been proven that this tax measure is difficult to set up administratively. This is true because wood products, for example, pass through many stages before they become part of a house.
In addition to the administrative difficulties involved in setting up this tax, the Department of National Revenue has changed the rules and regulations to my knowledge on at least two occasions, and perhaps more often than that. All these companies dealing in building materials have had difficulties with their initial assessments, and have then found that when the rules are changed the tax collectors come back, perhaps a year or two later, and re-assess the tax. This has made life extraordinarily difficult for them.
November 12, 1968

Leaving all these difficulties aside, and- perhaps some of them have arisen because of our psychological aversion to paying taxes- the fact is that the 11 per cent sales tax piles up administrative costs for those companies which deal with these building materials. In this way the 11 per cent becomes a higher percentage in relation to the over-all cost of a new house.
I suggest that if houses cost from $1,500 to $3,000 more because of the sales tax and its side effects, taken in conjunction with the high mortgage rates which all of us have to pay these days, many people find themselves with $500 to $1,000 less than they need to buy their own homes. When the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) comes back from his travels, or interrupts them, perhaps he should drop in on his good friend the Minister of Finance and persuade him that the elimination of this 11 per cent sales tax is a practical step to be taken immediately. This would put the cost of housing within reach of tens of thousands more Canadians who are now grasping at ownership but not able to reach it.
The Minister of Transport has at many meetings in various cities referred to conventional wisdom when faced with this old problem of housing. Perhaps he has suggested the same old solution. I do not know what else there is but conventional wisdom in this field. I do not think there is anything new under the sun in this housing field. Perhaps the minister will be able to find some new plan or scheme that is entirely different. If he does, he will have our entire appreciation, but I suggest in the meantime the elimination of the sales tax is a practical first step.
I intend to save some of my remarks for another occasion, but I think the government will have to recognize that if certain steps are taken as outlined in this budget it will be more difficult to find mortgage money for home building. Let me read very quickly in this regard from part of an editorial that appeared in this morning's Montreal Gazette:
In the last federal budget, Mr. Benson, as the federal finance minister, imposed new, heavy taxes on the insurance companies. To compensate for the diminished income resulting from the new taxes, the insurance companies may shift more of their investments out of fixed-value, long term securities and into common shares.
The insurance companies are permitted under law to invest 25 per cent of their assets in stocks. They now have in stocks far less than this permissible percentage. By moving into stocks they may not only hope for capital gains but would have the benefit of the 20 per cent tax credit.
The Budget-Mr. Clermont
Mr. Benson has spoken of the wide tax reforms he may introduce in his next budget. If these reforms follow the recommendations of the Carter commission, they will increase the amount of the tax credit for the holders of common shares. This would of course have the effect of making fixed-value, long term investments, such as mortgages, still more unattractive.
This is a very substantial problem facing the minister and I suggest that consideration must now be given to the use of money sources such as the federal superannuation fund and the Canada Pension Plan fund in respect of the very important matter of housing.
Finally, let me again read this statement from the Canadian conference on housing, which I think should be adopted by all Canadian politicians, no matter where they serve:
The Canadian conference on housing (1968) declares that all Canadians have the right to be adequately housed, whether they can afford it or not.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
