speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin my remarks by recalling an event which occurred last September 12. On that day, the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) issued a postage stamp commemorating Henri Bourassa, nationalist leader, member of parliament, journalist and founder of the newspaper Le Devoir, to celebrate the centennial of his birth. Henri Bourassa was born in Montreal on September 1, 1868. As a very young child, he moved with his father to Montebello, a small municipality in the riding of Labelle. When he was 21, he was elected mayor of his municipality. He had been offered the nomination two years earlier, but he was unable then to meet the requirements of the law. In 1896, he was elected to the House of Commons as a Liberal member for the riding of La-belle, which he represented until 1905. In 1905, he decided to go into provincial politics. From 1926 to 1935, he was again elected to the House of Commons, this time as an independent member.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) opened last September 3 an exhibition presented by the public archives of the national library, thanks to the generosity of the Bourassa family, which let them have some very interesting exhibits. The exhibition is to continue until November 15, 1968 and is open to the public.
I should now like to quote some extracts from an editorial written by Claude Ryan
COMMONS DEBATES	November 12. 1968
The Budget-Mr. Clermont and published in Le Devoir on August 31, 1968.
A man independent by nature, Henri Bourassa had a taste of party politics at the beginning of his career. He very quickly moved away from them. His vocation lay elsewhere.
This vocation can best be summarized by two words. Bourassa had been born and was to spend his whole life fighting for freedom and justice.
Bourassa was the father not only of French-Canadian nationalism, but of Canadian nationalism. However, nationalism was never an end in itself for him. It was rather the form which his love of freedom and justice had to take at the time when he lived.
Mr. Speaker, I had the honour, on three occasions, to represent the former Labelle constituency. Once again, I take this occasion to thank the electors for this honour and also to thank the people of the new Gatineau constituency for their generous support on my election last June 25.
The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) would have preferred no doubt to present to the house a balanced budget for the fiscal years 1968-69 and 1969-70 without any increase in taxes. He was not in a position to do so because of supplementary expenditures resulting mainly from joint federal-provincial programs which are not under the immediate jurisdiction of this government as they are administered by the provinces.
However, in the field of secondary education, the federal participation for the fiscal year 1965-66 was $40 million which included a special rebate to the province of Quebec. We find that, for the current year, federal transfers and cash payments to the provinces are estimated at some $500 million, which is equivalent to 12 times the amount paid three years ago.
During the present fiscal year, expenditures for university and post-secondary education amount to approximately $138 million more than forecast. On the other hand, the Canada assistance plan will be $47 million more than was expected. In the case of hospitalization, Mr. Speaker, the figures indicate an increase of $45 million. These three joint programs amount to a grand total of $230 million.
Mr. Speaker, three major changes not included in the calculation of the tax structure committee alone add $675 million in costs incurred by the federal treasury, compared with the projections for 1968-69, especially equalization payments to the Atlantic provinces for provincial post-secondary educational programs and other related programs, in order to assist as much as possible the

provinces to rationalize social welfare and to distribute further the costs implied in the Canada assistance plan established in 1967. Therefore, the contribution of the federal government to joint expenses for social welfare has been raised from $211 million, as indicated by the projections of the tax structure committee to the present estimates of $413 million. As for the equalization payments to the Atlantic provinces, the projections of $410 million, will apparently reach $590 million. For provincial post-secondary educational programs and other related programs in 1966, the federal government accepted to pay 50 per cent of the operating costs. As a result, instead of expenses of $300 million in 1968-69, in accordance with the estimates, the total amount of the federal commitments to financial assistance for provincial education will have almost doubled, that is about $610 million. This does not include, Mr. Speaker, the huge expenses for adult education entirely paid by the federal government under a national program which will cost some $220 million this year.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has been wise, as far as the estimates of the present financial year are concerned, to have refrained from trying, through financial measures, to collect sufficient revenues to balance the budget. In fact, as he suggested, such measures would have been quite strict and would have been prejudicial to the Canadian economy.
With regard to the year 1969-70, he was realistic and quite brave, because he could have gone to the capital market and obtained the revenues necessary to make up the deficit but, the provinces, the school boards, the municipalities and the private interests would have had greater difficulties in getting the necessary funds which they need, with the possibility of paying a higher rate of interest. In certain quarters, the Minister of Finance is blamed for the fact that the social development tax of 2 per cent does not bring any additional revenues to the provinces. According to the minister, the tax amendments suggested in the 1968-69 budget will bring, for the year of 1969-70, sufficient income to balance the budget. Otherwise, he would have had to increase the taxes further in order to transfer some to the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, with regard to federal contributions to the provinces and municipalities, such as equalization payments, social welfare benefits, health insurance, winter works, expenditures concerning the Trans-Canada highway, post-secondary education,
November 12, 1968

tax transfers and so on, from 1961-62 to 196768, they went from $900 million to $2.6 billion, which is about 26 per cent instead of 15 per cent of the total federal budget expenditures. That has no relation with the regular increase in tax payments made to the provinces with regard to personal income tax, which have gone up from 16 to 28 per cent, that is from $641 million to $1,829 million.
Mr. Speaker, the minister has announced on various occasions that, in 1969, the government will have to put before parliament a proposal to revise the taxation system in depth. I hope that this so-called social development tax of 2 per cent-the 3 per cent surtax levied since the beginning of the current year is supposed to end on December 31, 1969-will also come to an end on that date and that this revision will eliminate discrimination with regard to income tax.
Many criticisms have been made about the ceiling of $120 on that so-called social development tax of 2 per cent. But, Mr. Speaker, there have been precedents with regard to the maximum.
In 1951, when the old age security pension was adopted, a tax of 2 per cent was introduced with a ceiling of $60, and now this ceiling is $240. In 1965, when parliament voted for an abatement of 10 per cent on income tax, a maximum amount of $600 was also set. Similarly, with regard to the Canada pension, plan, we have a minimum income of $600 and a ceiling of $5,000 which will be raised to $5,200 on January 1, 1969.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw this to the attention of the Minister of Finance. Other members have mentioned the fact that some people have to spend part of their income on such things as tools, equipment, books, even clothing in certain cases, and on transportation costs to get to work, and the fact that those deductions are allowed companies and the self-employed.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
In this connection, here are few remarks and proposals made by the royal commission on taxation. I quote a few excerpts from volume 3, page 289:
We now turn to consider the deduction of expenses by employees. The principle involved is clear enough. All the expenses incurred in the expectation of generating net gains, other than personal living expenses, should be allowed as deductions from all actual gross gains. Distinctions between the kinds and forms of taxable gains, and considerations of whether a net gain actually resulted from the expenditures, are irrelevant. The major problem would be to allow the deduction of all expenses laid out to generate employment income and yet to prevent the deduction of personal living expenses.

The Budget-Mr. Clermont
I shall now quote from page 312 of the same volume:
We came to the conclusion that the most equitable course would be to treat employment income on the same basis as income from a business or profession. Expenses would then be deductible if reasonably related to the earning of income. The prohibition against the deduction of personal and living expenses as set out in section 12(1) (h) of the Income Tax Act would, of course, be applicable, as would the provision in section 12(2) that expenses must be reasonable in the circumstances.
The deductibility of particular itemized expenses would then be determined in accordance with the rules to be applied to business expenses. Employees, like the self-employed, would not be permitted to deduct travelling and entertainment expenses in excess of the limits discussed earlier in this chapter.
Mr. Speaker, these expenses could be considered as acceptable to the extent of 3 per cent of the gross income or a maximum of $500. Any person having expenses over $500 could deduct them, with supporting proofs.
I would like also to deal with the legislation on small businesses loans, amended in 1967, to enable more owners of small businesses to take advantage of it. Another amendment would increase from $250,000 to $500,000 the approximate yearly income maximum required of a borrower. At the present time, a borrower may get a maximum of $25,000 only, a ceiling established in 1961 when this legislation came into force, to enable the owner of a small business to consider a substantial expansion of his enterprise. But in 1968 such a maximum is unrealistic, and this amount must necessarily be increased.
Moreover, the section on the 5J per cent maximum interest rate should be amended. I recognize that it is very important for heads of businesses to secure loans, but how good is a 5J per cent interest rate if bank managers find all kinds of reasons to refuse these loans?
As we all know, Mr. Speaker, this house very recently changed the farm loan corporation interest rate. It was 5 per cent. The farm improvement loan rate was also changed.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the minister of Finance should give serious consideration to my remarks and I think he could amend this section on interest rates without a review of the legislation by parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I would like once more to bring forth a matter I wish to deal with in this house. It has been raised by several members and has to do with water pollution.
November 12, 1968

The Budget-Mr. Penner
Our area is affected by the pollution of the Ottawa River and of its tributaries. According to a study of the salubrity of the river, issued by the Ontario Water Resources Commission it has been found, in several places along the river, between Pembroke and Hawkesbury, that the water was not up to the required standards and that taking the necessary steps to control it would involve considerable expenditures which are far beyond the financial means of the municipalities concerned.
The Association quebecoise des techniques de l'eau has held on February 12, 13, 14, 15 and 16, its fifth annual Congress, at the Sheraton Mount Royal Hotel, in Montreal.
The theme of that conference "Water, everyone's problem" was intended to illustrate that everyone should fully assume his responsibilities, if our society wishes to achieve the progress necessary to promote the rational use of water.
In the Realties magazine about a year or so ago, a questionnaire was submitted to 25 Nobel Prize winners as well as to 25 of the world's prominent figures. One of the questions was: In your opinion, what are the most serious problems which the world will have to face within the next 20 years? The answers showed that population explosion was considered as the most serious problem; it was generally thought that such an explosion would cause food shortages, and poverty in under-developed countries and, furthermore, that man and industry would pollute water almost irretrievably unless a drastic change in the present approach concerning the use of that basic resource be implemented.
Conservation of water is everyone's problem. Therefore, governments, municipalities, industries and citizens in particular must fully assume their responsibilities.
We must get rid of an idea which is voiced too often by too many people; "Such and such an industry or municipality has yet to do something, so why me?" Too often, as result of this attitude no one does anything and our rivers continue to go out to the sea as they have always done, but with this difference that along the river, homes, industries and cities repeatedly use their drop of water.
Public opinion is already sensitized to the important problem of water pollution. Still, it is imperative that the people understand that solutions are difficult to find as well as costly.

In every country, the critical problem is that of finding the financial resources to be applied in a fight against pollution. It has been established that it would cost approximately $500 million to purify the waters for all Quebec municipalities with a population of 5,000 or more, and approximately $300 million to do the same for the smaller municipalities.
That is why financing the struggle against water pollution requires close co-operation between provincial and federal governments because the municipalities and cities do not have the required financial resources to solve this serious problem.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a representative from northwestern Ontario, an area which constitutes slightly more than half of the land and water mass of the entire province and rivals each of the three prairie provinces in size, I wish to limit my remarks in this budget debate to the topic of regional economic development, with particular reference to the mid-Canada corridor concept. There has been a revolution in Canada's thinking about northern development. It was only a decade ago that a royal commission on Canada's economic prospects described as unfavourable the outlook for northern development. They could not see a very close analogy between the historical opening of the west and the similar pressure now for economic development of the north.
Frequently, northern Ontario has been referred to as an economic desert, conveying to us the impression that this great central part of our country is forever doomed to remain unpeopled and unproductive. In his history of Canada, Stephen Leacock more than 20 years ago wrote this:
Perhaps the brightest page in these annals, is the record of discovery and exploration of the incalculable mineral wealth of the central wilderness of Canada between Hudson bay and the lakes. This means far more than the wealth itself, great though it must he, for it removes from our commonwealth its fatal geographical defect of an uninhabited and seemingly worthless central area which broke east and west apart.
Dr. Leacock's prophecy of a flourishing north has not yet been fulfilled, but many experts now believe that Canada's future is inseparably linked with the development of natural resources in the north. This vast undeveloped and most important area has the potential to support millions of people. The
November 12, 1968
advent of new and easier forms of transportation, better and cheaper systems of communication and modern technology applied to township development, carry the promise of considerable economic activity and settlement in Canada's north, this treasurehouse of national resources.
Recent economic studies and conferences have established that there are a number of problems in the development of the north which must be tackled. I should like to refer to just a few of these, Mr. Speaker. The first, and probably most important, is the availability of markets. Nothing can be done, no matter how rich and vast the resources, unless we have markets. This is more important to the north than to any other part of Canada. Resources will have to be developed, and on a large scale, in order to recover costs. Therefore large markets are needed, most of them outside of Canada. We must be widely concerned with the development of markets and our relations with countries which are going to be our markets, particularly I think the United States of America.
Second in the way of problems is the availability of capital. Most northern development involves very heavy investment of capital. Our future circumstances are not likely to be easy in this respect. We will live in a world of scarcity of capital for some time to come. There will be many competing demands for capital elsewhere, so if the north is going to develop it must be able to compete. We must have policies applied to the north, and to the country as a whole, that will attract capital. Capital has far less nationality now than at any time in the past, and it will go where the attractions are the greatest. In Canada the question of long term opportunity and security are very important.
Third in the way of problems is manpower. We face manpower problems in the north with which we in Canada have not had much experience. Northern development must proceed in a way that will give native peoples a future in their own country. However, nowhere in the past in Canada have we carried out economic development on the basis of involving the native people to any great extent. The danger is that economic development will run far ahead of the ability of native people to participate. We must do everything possible to shorten the time required to educate them sufficiently.
The fourth problem is transportation. Fortunately, there have been major new developments in transportation that offer great promise, although they still remain to be adapted
The Budget-Mr. Penner to the particular problems of the north. In the meantime we must rely heavily upon rail transportation. Other areas of Canada have received great assistance in their development by means of specific subsidies from the federal government for reduction of freight rates in their respective territories. There is a precedent therefore for similar consideration of the needs of northwestern Ontario, as part of a national economic development policy. In the clamorous contention for equality, the just and reasonable demands of this great central section of Canada have gone unheard and unheeded. Its promise, therefore, has remained largely unfulfilled as a result.
The fifth problem is that of efficiency. The north will always be a high cost area. In the past, Canada has had a habit of letting other countries, particularly the United States, solve its development problems. But in this case, in the development of our north, Canada will have to make more than her customary effort to solve her own problems. Fortunately we can now use technology more extensively than in past development. The basis of research and development is already set up in our universities but we have not a big background in this respect as yet.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
I wish now to make a few comments, Mr. Speaker, regarding what has become known in some circles as the mid-Canada corridor concept. The long range development of a coast to coast corridor through Canada's midnorth would go a long way to meet both the opportunities and the problems that have been outlined. Such a concept has been advanced in a corridor running from Newfoundland through Labrador, northern Quebec south of James bay, the northern Ontario clay belt, northern Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta and into three arms-one stretching up the Mackenzie valley of the Northwest Territories, another into the Yukon, and the third into northern British Columbia. It generally runs between the narrow belt in which 90 per cent of Canadians live and what is considered to be the far north, and varies in width between 200 and 500 miles.
The Canada north development corridor is identified as an area with the following general characteristics: The climate is acceptable to working and living; the terrain is accessible and suitable for development; resources are abundant and well distributed; settlements already exist; there are potential urban growth centres; north-south transportation

November 12, 1968

The Budget-Mr. Penner routes already reach into the areas; and finally, new east-west transportation routes can be provided in a reasonable manner.
Preliminary study supports the concept of a coast to coast Canada north development corridor, Mr. Speaker, and a number of reasons are advanced to support the claim. Canada is expected to become a giant among the productive nations of the world, thus its future is inseparably linked with the development of the north. Such a development would require people, capital resources, foresight and initiative. It could be a challenge that would truly shape our destiny; a Canadian undertaking, financed by public and private funds and part of an overall national planning policy.
Of great consequence will be those elements of the national policy which direct economic activity and capital to certain specific areas in the development corridor. Northwestern Ontario is now ready to receive such special attention. It is obvious that the conscious creation and implementation of a Canada north development corridor concept as outlined must be a national undertaking, requiring vast amounts of public and private capital and manpower, and the support of the people of Canada as a national objective over the next several decades.
The provision of adequate incentives to bring industry and people into the area will play an important role in the establishment of the development corridor. Incentives for industry may vary from direct financial subsidies to the provision of tax regulations, and a transportation rate structure to allow new industries to operate competitively. Incentives for settlers may include high incomes, good employment opportunities, long holidays, and urban settlements of sufficient size with a wide range of services and amenities-perhaps a climatically controlled environment and good and inexpensive transportation linkages to other settlements in Canada north and south. While the rate of development in Canada north will, to a large extent, depend on the demand for its resources, the rate of development will also greatly depend upon a national policy which expresses the kind of nation in which Canadians wish to live.
Concrete plans to develop the concept are already in progress, Mr. Speaker. A two-part conference will explore the feasibility and that were first presented in a 1967 report. The conference will explore the feasibility and practicability of the development plan, and held in conjunction with it will be field trips to Siberia and northern Sweden.
The conference will be sponsored by the University of Guelph, Lakehead University, Laurentian University and the Ontario government. It has grown from a vision of Richard Rohmer now a Toronto lawyer, who last year commissioned a research project by a prominent and well known research and planning firm of Toronto. The opening session of the conference will be held at Lakehead University next January 18 and 19. The second meeting, after the field trips, will be held in August 1969.
The federal government has agreed to support and participate in the conference, Mr. Speaker. The provinces and territories through which the corridor passes will also be asked to join as co-sponsors. Representatives of industry, labour, finance and commerce will also be invited to take part. The ultimate findings of the conference will be submitted to the governments involved for them to initiate further studies and policy leading to action.
To dramatize the project, a film has been prepared which is entitled "Leave this not to Cain". The title refers to Jacques Cartier's purported comment that the Canadian north was the land that God gave to the first murderer. The film unreels photographic and factual evidence that this is no wasteland, and that modern technology can make northern living comfortable and give it a distinctive appeal. It asserts that Canada is fortunate to have such a frontier, with its potential attraction for the restless young in search of a challenge. The film concludes:
It is here, after all, that we will forge an identity. The land will form us. It will stamp us with its uniqueness. Always, from the beginning, it has been a bequest, the sort of gift a future can hinge on-the future of a whole people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the occasion of my first speech in this house, I should like to congratulate you on your unanimous re-election as Speaker of this house. Canada is fortunate in having been able to have you presiding over the proceedings of its legislators. Your integrity and your dignity represent the ideal required of leaders by the institutions of our parliamentary system. It is with admiration that I support the choice of this house.
I think it is suitable to point out the outstanding contribution of the Hon. Hedard Robichaud to the public affairs of Canada. I feel particularly proud of having been elected as the successor of a man so dedicated to his fellow citizens and to his country, I also

November 12, 1968

wish to express my admiration and respect for the premier of New Brunswick, the Hon. Louis J. Robichaud. The eagerness and courage with which he is serving New Brunswick show he is a great Canadian.
I also wish to express my most sincere appreciation to the right hon. Prime Minister, Mr. Pierre-Elliott Trudeau; he understands Canada and he is a real Canadian.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
His leadership answers the aspirations of young Canadians and the needs of our country.
Since the house is now studying the budget speech, I would like to assure the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) of my wholehearted support for his fiscal and budgetary changes.
This budget, Mr. Speaker, is realistic. It fights against inflation. It is unfortunate that the government should have to take steps to restrain development and diminish the purchasing power of the Canadian people. However, let us not forget that inflation always follows a boom which upsets the economic balance.
Certain members on the other side of the house have criticized this budget. They accuse the government of being irresponsible and bring forward all sorts of arguments, all of them unrealistic, in order to attract public attention.
To impose taxes is a difficult and complex job, Mr. Speaker.
However, I must remind those members that the Canadian people had the opportunity to listen to them and to their colleagues in the party before last June 25, and that on that date it chose the party it wanted. In my opinion, they are wasting their time trying to have their inconsistent fiscal policy adopted. They say that government expenditure is too high. However, they did not refrain from making promises during the last election campaign. I wonder how they would have managed to keep them without increasing expenditures or reducing certain services. Mr. Speaker, their attitude is completely illogical.
It is customary, I believe, for a member making his maiden speech in the House of Commons to talk about his riding. I should like to speak particularly about the future of the riding of Gloucester in view of the efforts made by the government to reduce the economic gap between the Atlantic provinces and the rest of the country.
The Budget-Mr. Breau
The economic situation of the constituency of Gloucester is not flourishing because of a great number of factors. First, we are struck by the importance of the economic gap existing between the Atlantic provinces and the rest of Canada, and my constituency is badly affected. In short, from the economic point of view the geographic situation of the constituency of Gloucester is not so favourable as that of the other Atlantic provinces.
Another factor which is prejudicial to our economy is the psychological climate of the population. It is true that in a certain part of the constituency, namely the Bathurst region, wages are reasonable and maybe even appropriate. We find there a psychological climate more favourable to investment and, therefore, to economic development. Generally, that region is the most prosperous of the constituency.
However, as far as the rest of the constituency is concerned, the greatest part of its population is composed of fishermen, farmers or lumberjacks. We have seen in the economic history of other countries that people in such trades are not attracted by economic development. That economic situation is detrimental to the cultural and social progress of people and therefore there is a real danger of losing a great deal of skills which are so necessary to our country.
The fishing industry, at the present time, is having a hard time. Because of the unfavourable market situation, the prices paid to the fishermen are relatively low. Even under normal circumstances, fishing now requires technological studies and investment. The small fisherman-there are several of them in my riding-is still placed in a dilemma and lives in frustrating economic conditions.
Weather and soil conditions in our area are not very favourable to farming. Consequently, unless modem techniques are being developed in order to improve this situation, the small farmers in my area must forget about that avenue, or engage in it through sheer love of the thing or to provide for their own needs. It should be mentioned also that the main market for food products is located far away. Therefore one can reasonably say that farming at the present time is not a viable industry for the Gloucester riding.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
As far as lumber operations are concerned, mechanization now eliminates the lumbermen. They are therefore forced to get into another field of work, which is very difficult for them.

November 12, 1968
The Budget-Mr. Breau
The conditions I have just mentioned, Mr. Speaker, are well known to hon. members but, in my opinion, it is my duty to bring them up.
The federal government has done a lot already to improve the situation in my riding and to reduce the economic gap between the Atlantic provinces and the rest of Canada. In fact, two years ago, the government of New Brunswick and the federal government reached an agreement under which the latter undertook to co-operate in the implementation of a rural development program.
The news was very well received but after a while, since they had not understood the real meaning of the program, the people felt frustrated by the lack of visible results. The program I am talking about is only breaking ground for a real development scheme. It is a pilot project, therefore a program that will serve as a guide for subsequent programs. That program will have to make the population more conscious of development. If the people of the riding of Gloucester take part in the pilot project now under way, they will be ready to take advantage of other programs. They will see to it that those programs reach their objectives more easily and are consequently more advantageous for Canada.
The citizens of Gloucester were very happy to hear the Prime Minister say that the problem of national unity will not be solved as long as economic disparities have not been abolished in Canada. They have been waiting to hear those words for a long time, because they want to be first class Canadians. Therefore, the creation of a Department of Regional Development makes me very happy.
I read with great interest the remarks made by the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Marchand) before the Atlantic Development Board in Halifax on October 29 last. I commend him for the serious and realistic way with which he faces his challenge. To reduce the economic disparities between provinces, it is essential to initiate a well-planned study, geared towards a common objective. I mean by that that the federal, provincial and municipal governments, in short the whole population, must develop an objective to which everyone must hold fast.
The operation of the new department is now confined to the co-ordination of the efforts of the various departments, while appraising the markets for viable industries and preparing the various avenues necessary for development. But in my opinion, the minister must see to it that the government fiscal and

budgetary policies make allowance for regional circumstances. He should also, in conjunction with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hel-lyer), set up a more realistic policy concerning the transportation problems in the area.
The department will also have to consider the possibility for the federal government to have a greater concentration of its purchasing power in the Atlantic provinces. For instance, it should encourage industries, which are government suppliers, to settle in that area. The government national policies have not promoted progress in the Atlantic provinces in the past. I do not say that the future Department of Regional Development should not go beyond those three suggestions. Those are simply three examples of decisions which could stimulate the economy of the area. It will then be easier for the department to find means of reducing the economic disparities which exist, and to that end, it should provide for the establishment of basic guidelines concerning the maximum use of manpower by training a qualified and mobile manpower and increasing the quantity and the quality of jobs. It is a pity that most of the workers in our area should, at a certain age, have to leave the province in order to go somewhere else in Canada, or which is worse, to the United States.
We must also control the maximum development of the production potential of the Atlantic provinces through education, training and retraining and develop all human resources. Moreover, we must provide for accessibility to production technology, for the establishment of economic growth centres, for the orderly and planned use of financing as well as human capital.
The minister must also ensure the availability of essential services for the villages and towns that are potential industrial centres.
Encouragement must also be given to creative economic activities, use of an adequate and modern technology and development of viable economic activities.
Finally, we must see to the full development of our tourist resources and to the establishment of essential facilities for tourism.

The six principles that the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Marchand) has expressed to the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council are the essence of a very realistic plan. Of particular importance is the fifth principle mentioning the importance of
November 12, 1968

the people's participation. People must indeed become involved in this rural development. The whole scheme must be an effort of the entire population. Without that it will fail.

I should mention here the efforts made by the Conseil regional d'amenagement du Nord and The Northern Regional Development Council. Those councils of my district must ensure a minimum of support on the part of the population. They must really help the population to go through the psychological changes necessary to the development and, therefore, should be careful not to confuse people. They must inform people, explain to them the real meaning of the present projects and their relationship to future projects.
The lessening of the economic gap existing between the Atlantic provinces and the rest of Canada will have the effect of encouraging and reassuring the people of my district, but as the future Minister of Regional Development said, we shall not see the tangible results of this before some fifteen years.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The elite of today may still enjoy better conditions but it is not the elite which suffers the most today. It is true that it does not enjoy conditions comparable to those of their equals in the centre of Canada, but it is the small fishermen, farmers and lumberjacks I have mentioned who do not profit by the prosperous economy.
The few fishermen who are lucky enough to participate in the development of their industry, those who work at the paper mill of Bathurst, or in the mines or at the foundry of Bathurst may have a sufficient income. But the less fortunate will not participate in this development.
Most of them are between 25 and 60 and what is unfortunate is that the social assistance scheme does not solve their problems. Social assistance cannot-and I pray heaven that it will not-become a substitute for employment.
Even though our labour force is unskilled, it must be gainfully employed in order to avoid the danger of having unemployed people. I think that the government social assistance programs are obviously essential, but there must be some assurance that these programs are benefiting those in need of them and are not being used to destroy the people's initiative.
The Budget-Mr. Breau
I think the Minister of Regional Development will be in a position to collaborate with the Minister of National Health and Welfare in order to establish regional policies ensuring social security as criteria vary with the different regions.
Regional criteria differ in rural areas from those in urban areas. The department must take future planning into account, because regional development in the interest of the population and economic progress call for planning: it is not done on short notice. In the meantime, short term solutions must be found in order to assist the less fortunate and those are two factors which are quite different.
Mr. Speaker, as the member representing Canadians of the Gloucester constituency, I wish to convey to the right hon. Prime Minister and to his government the assurance of my full co-operation.
I want to remind the hon. members that I am interested in the development of the Atlantic provinces for one good reason: because it is essential to Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Rising to speak in this budget debate makes me sad, Mr. Speaker. I would like to speak in support of the budget, because I am sure the government has done its best, but I find there is precious little cheerful news in it for anybody, and certainly not for my constituents in Battle River. All the budget promises them is sweat, taxes and tears-their sweat their taxes, and Mr. Benson's tears.
To hear our Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) weep over the terrible state of the federal government's finances is enough to soften the hardest heart, until of course you remember that he and his colleagues are the authors of their own misfortunes. However, he was able to choke back his sobs long enough to be able to announce that all of us will have to pay a new 2 per cent surtax on our incomes. He said this was necessary because federal finances were in such bad shape, and admittedly they are. He was very eloquent when he pleaded for everyone to cut back spending and save money, but certainly we have no evidence that the government is considering restraint in its administrative costs.
The Auditor General has reported that $2J million is being paid out by three federal departments for new office accommodation, and an additional $1 million for equipment, I would gather mostly for prestige. Then, Mr. Speaker, there is that door hanging at the back of the centre block of the parliament buildings. It does not really look that much different from a great many other doors I have seen-I do not believe you could even drive a combine through it-but there must be something different about it because I notice we paid over $13,000 for it.
The Minister of Finance did not mention that while the government is supposed to be setting an example to the country and to individual taxpayers on how to save money, his colleagues in the cabinet are living high, wide and handsome at the taxpayers' expense. I would like to recall something that Thomas Jefferson said almost 200 years ago:
I place economy among the first and most important virtues and public debt as the greatest of dangers to pursue our independence. We must not ourselves load up with perpetual debt. We must make our choice between economy and liberty, or profusion and servitude. If we can prevent the government from wasting the labours of the people under the pretence of caring for them, they will be happy. The same prudence which in private life would forbid our paying our money for unexplained projects, forbids it in the use of public money.
The minister did not mention the money that would be spent this year on the B and B
[Mr. Deputy Speaker.)
DEBATES	November 12, 19G8
commission, a mere few hundreds of thousands of dollars on top of the $7 million already spent on it. He skipped quickly over the fact that not every Canadian taxpayer will pay the full 2 per cent on his or her income. Only those earning less than $10,000 per year will pay the full charge. This country of ours, this bulwark of the just society is supposed to provide the same opportunity for all, with no discrimination; yet three quarters of our taxpayers will be paying an additional 2 per cent while about one quarter will pay considerably less.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
As an illustration I will take an income of $4,000. On this an individual will pay a tax increase of $80. A man with an income of $40,000 will pay a tax of $120. The man with an income of $4,000 pays 2 per cent. The man with an income of $40,000 pays one third of one per cent. On top of all this the Prime Minister announced publicly that he would be trying to find ways to lighten the tax burden on the higher income groups. The Minister of Finance called the new surcharge on income a social development tax, but I am sure if his boss has his way and high incomes are to have their tax rate cut back we can look forward to getting hit with additional taxes in the next budget. The Minister of Finance probably will call it a poverty development tax, because if he and his friends keep going the way they are they will be turning all of us into the new Canadian poor.
This new tax perhaps would not have been so hard to take if it was really what he said it was, a social development tax. If some of that 2 per cent tax revenue was to be paid out for higher old age pensions, social assistance or veterans allowances, it would be justified. If it were put on our backs to help the people in our society who need real help just to stay alive at today's prices and with today's inflation, we might be happy to pay it. When we speak of inflation we must remember that no civilized country in the world ever adopted the extreme philosophies of either fascism or communism unless the middle class was first liquidated by inflation.
This was a desperation budget. Five years of uncontrolled and irresponsible spending by the federal government left the till empty. Desperate measures had to be taken to raise ready cash. The first and obvious step was to load a bigger income tax on the group of citizens least able to resist or talk back. That explains the 2 per cent surtax and the cut-off at incomes of $10,000. Our finance minister
November 12, 1968	COMMONS
then looked around at the next most helpless group, and found the old reliable area, the dead. Sure, he made estates passing between husband and wife exempt from taxation, but at the same time he more than received the money back by finagling the taxation rate on other estates.
Then of course we must look at the plight of those engaged in western agriculture. The men of the west are experiencing one of the most trying times in their history. People are selling their farms; some are hungry, and I might say that in respect of those that are not hungry or selling out, if conditions do not soon improve the nation will see one of the greatest bank robberies in history. But, no, we cannot afford an acreage payment or a subsidy for the farmers of the west. Under a previous Conservative government acreage payment cost the federal treasury approximately $46 million in one year. This was of immeasureable help to many people in buying their groceries throughout the winter.
This government has already spent $46 million on the national arts centre, that Liberal granite memorial across the street here. While I am dwelling on the figure of $46 million another matter comes to mind, which also concerns a matter of approximately $46 million. I refer now to our Canada 3 per cent perpetual bond issue of the dirty thirties. People who were patriotic bought these bonds because they had faith in the future and faith in the integrity of our country. I am sure, however, that their generous gesture did not include a gift of money to Canada for all time. After all it was a loan with interest to be paid at 3 per cent and every loan must have a maturity date. In this case the date was 30 years hence, or 1966. Any other financial arrangement that is even hinted at is completely out of reason. The subsequent events of 1966, the extending of the maturity date another 30 years at 3 per cent interest, in my opinion was an attempted swindle, the result of a blatant confidence game which if perpetrated by private enterprise would be investigated immediately, and penitentiary sentences would be handed out to those who instigated such a crime. We have had explained to us by our previous finance minister the reason it was not paid back; but let us not stand for any mamby-pamby financial jargon, because the facts are clear.
The facts are that the government of Canada asked for a loan from its citizens; it promised to pay 3 per cent on that loan until maturity after 30 years, or 1966 in this case.
DEBATES	2673
The Budget-Mr. Downey It refused to honour its debt. The market price has nothing to do with the value of the actual debt. Our government owes the people the face value of this loan. In my opinion this is a very serious matter, and one of principle which rises above academic political thinking. Something must be done, and done now, because we cannot let the integrity of Canada rot at the seams for the sake of the price of this granite museum across the street which, I might add, most Canadians will never see. If we are to expect the people of Canada to have confidence in our debt and to buy future bond issues, then we had better give them something on which to base their confidence.
Franklin D. Roosevelt said in 1932 in respect of debt that any government, like any family, can for a year spend a little more than it earns; but you and I know that continuance of that habit means the poorhouse. I think this holds just as true today as it did in 1932. All this is unpleasant and depressing, but I believe the worst feature of the Benson budget is its negative, defeatist spirit. It makes no provision for national development, for assistance to agriculture, for our export trade, or for our vital resource and service industries. It is an open admission of surrender to the influence of big business, and a shameful confession that the minister and his colleagues have neither the heart nor the guts to do the things that are necessary for Canada today.
It is not news to anybody that this government has written off the small farmer and the small businessman. So far as Ottawa is concerned, they have been classed as expendable for five years now. But it is news, and grim news at that, that the government by the terms of this budget appears to have written off the whole area of Canadian agriculture and large sectors of other vital basic industries. The members of the government appear content to sit tight in their Ottawa offices, raising money by taxes and loans while prices climb, inflation grows and interest rates soar. They appear to be unconscious of the fact that most Canadians are overburdened by taxes, frustrated by lack of government policy and action, and are growing increasingly depressed about the future.
In closing I should like to reiterate the sentiments expressed by one hon. member the other day. It would seem that to be a financial expert today is to pass our financial troubles on to future generations. No progress will be made in getting out of this financial morass in which we are mired until we

November 12, 1968
Ways and Means
accept the responsibility of paying the debts of our time in our time.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I suppose to suggest here today that we as a nation should pay our way would label me as a bit of a square, but we all know what happens in the business field if we spend more than we make. I see no reason why the principles of business management should not also apply to the business of this nation.

It being twelve minutes before ten o'clock, by unanimous consent Mr. Speaker adjourned the house, without question put.

Wednesday, November 13, 1968
